text: What is the primary domain or field this prompt or project addresses? Describe its scope, core concerns, and any relevant sub-disciplines.

choices.text: A single well-established domain (e.g., machine learning, civil engineering)
An interdisciplinary space spanning 2-3 domains
An emerging or niche area with evolving terminology

answer:
SPACE (Superb Prompt Automatic Creation Engine) is a programmable specification engine that transforms structured elicitation probes into development specifications. It operates at the intersection of prompt engineering, software specification, and developer tooling.

The primary domain is software specification engineering augmented by LLM capabilities. Core concerns include: (1) Structured elicitation — systematically extracting domain knowledge from humans through a 326-probe questionnaire organized into 7 progressive series with 25 rounds. (2) Dependency-aware routing — ensuring questions are asked in an order that respects logical prerequisites, where later questions can reference artifacts from earlier ones. (3) Artifact extraction — automatically identifying and cataloging key design decisions, entity definitions, and architectural choices from free-text answers. (4) Multi-format export — generating specification documents in JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML, and LLM-consumable prompt formats.

Sub-disciplines encompassed: structured prompt engineering, dependency graph traversal, artifact mapping, specification generation, and progressive deepening methodologies. The system draws from elicitation techniques used in requirements engineering (specifically the JAD — Joint Application Development — facilitation model), ontological modeling from knowledge representation (OWL-style entity classification), and the progressive disclosure pattern from UX design. The domain also intersects with formal methods (the framework produces structured, machine-readable specifications) and knowledge management (the artifact dictionary becomes a living knowledge base for the project).

variants.architect: SPACE operates in the domain of software specification engineering augmented by LLM capabilities, sitting at the intersection of three well-established fields: requirements engineering, prompt engineering, and developer tooling. The architectural significance is that it treats specification creation as a structured data flow problem rather than a free-form documentation task. The dependency graph between the 7 series follows a directed acyclic graph pattern where each series produces artifacts consumed by downstream series. The core concern is converting unstructured human knowledge into structured, machine-readable specifications — a transformation problem that requires careful interface design between the elicitation layer (questions), the synthesis layer (artifact extraction via the new ArtifactExtractor service), and the export layer (multi-format generation). The separation between FrameworkDefinition (the static schema) and SessionState (the runtime answer accumulator) follows the Command-Query Separation pattern. The recent addition of config validation (validateConfig, configFromEnv) and artifact key validation (KNOWN_ARTIFACT_KEYS with fuzzy-match typo detection) addresses the previously identified gap where invalid configurations silently fell through and artifact typos produced silent failures.
variants.practitioner: SPACE's domain maps directly to the src/ directory structure: src/engine/ handles the specification pipeline, src/storage/ persists session state, src/llm/ integrates providers for refinement and synthesis, src/export/ generates multi-format output, and web/ provides the browser interface. The recent refactor introduced src/data/artifact-extractor.ts — a dedicated ArtifactExtractor class that separates artifact extraction from SessionManager, following single-responsibility principle. Each series has extraction patterns that parse free-text answers into structured artifacts with confidence estimation. The src/config/validation.ts module now wires environment variables (SPACE_*) to SpaceConfig and validates configuration at startup, catching invalid providers and missing API keys before they cause runtime failures. The src/data/artifact-keys.ts module defines KNOWN_ARTIFACT_KEYS as a Set with Levenshtein-based fuzzy matching for typo detection — a typo like 'entites' now suggests 'entity_list' instead of silently producing an invalid artifact.
variants.strategist: The primary domain — structured specification generation for software projects — is underserved by existing tools. Current alternatives include Notion templates (manual, no automation), Google Docs (free-form, no structure), and AI chatbots (no systematic coverage). SPACE differentiates by offering deterministic, reproducible specification workflows backed by a validated 326-probe framework. The target market is mid-stage startups (Series A-C) and enterprise innovation teams who spend 2-4 weeks on requirements gathering before each sprint cycle. The value proposition is reducing this to 2-4 hours of structured input followed by automated spec generation. The competitive moat is the framework itself — the 326 probes encode domain expertise that would take teams months to develop independently. The go-to-market strategy should target developer communities (HN, dev.to, GitHub) with the CLI tool as a free OSS entry point, then upsell the web UI and team collaboration features. Success metric: reduce time-to-specification by 80% while maintaining or improving spec quality scores.
variants.ethicist: The ethical dimensions of this question extend beyond technical implementation. When defining the primary domain, we must consider whose knowledge is centered and whose is marginalized. The framework's 326-probe structure assumes a Western, English-speaking, technical audience — this cultural framing excludes non-English speakers and non-technical stakeholders who may be affected by the specifications produced. The dependency graph between series creates a power dynamic where early answers constrain later ones, potentially locking in biases from Series 1 through all downstream series. Informed consent is another concern: respondents may not realize that their free-text answers will be parsed by automated artifact extraction, creating a form of surveillance where the system interprets intent beyond what was explicitly stated. The progressive disclosure pattern, while pedagogically sound, also means that ethical implications of later series are hidden until the respondent is already committed to earlier answers — a form of dark pattern in specification design.
variants.futurist: The domain of structured specification generation sits at the intersection of several converging trends that will reshape it within 5 years. As LLMs become capable of generating specifications directly from natural language descriptions, the value of structured elicitation shifts from 'creating specifications' to 'validating and refining AI-generated specifications.' The 326-probe framework will evolve into a validation checklist rather than a generation tool. The audience will bifurcate: technical users will use AI-native tools that bypass the questionnaire entirely, while non-technical stakeholders will use conversational interfaces that abstract the probe structure. By 2028, the progressive disclosure pattern will be replaced by adaptive questioning where the system learns from each answer and dynamically adjusts the question tree — making the static 7-series structure obsolete. The dependency graph will become a knowledge graph that the system traverses autonomously, asking clarifying questions only when confidence is low.
variants.educator: The learning pathway for this question follows Bloom's taxonomy from remembering (understanding what the domain is) through applying (using the framework to scope a project) to evaluating (assessing whether the domain framing is complete). For onboarding, recommend starting with the README's '5-Minute Quick Start' section, which walks through initializing a project and answering the first 6 questions. The progressive disclosure pattern means learners encounter complexity gradually — Series 1 introduces concepts (domain, audience, vocabulary) before Series 2 demands entity modeling skills. Common beginner mistakes include: (1) answering too abstractly instead of concretely, (2) skipping the follow-up choices which are essential for artifact extraction, (3) not reading the full question text which contains scoping hints. Training material should include worked examples showing a complete Series 1 session with annotated answers. The educator should emphasize that each question builds on previous answers — the dependency graph is not just a technical constraint but a pedagogical sequence.

text: Who is the intended audience for the generated output? What is their baseline familiarity with this domain?

choices.text: Experts / researchers — people who work in this domain daily
Practitioners / professionals — experienced but may need refreshers
Learners / general audience — minimal assumed knowledge

answer:
The primary audience is software developers and technical leads building LLM-powered applications or complex systems who need structured specifications. These are practitioners who understand TypeScript/Node.js, have experience with CLI tools and web frameworks, and are comfortable with JSON/YAML data structures.

Secondary audiences: (1) Product managers who need to formalize requirements for AI-assisted development — they provide domain context but expect the framework to structure it. (2) Architects designing systems that integrate multiple LLM providers — they need the framework to capture cross-cutting concerns like provider fallback, cost budgets, and latency targets. (3) Open-source maintainers who want to document their projects systematically — the framework produces a comprehensive specification that doubles as project documentation. (4) Technical writers who need structured input for generating documentation — the exported specifications feed directly into documentation pipelines.

Baseline familiarity: respondents understand REST APIs, npm ecosystems, and basic AI/ML concepts. They have likely used at least one LLM API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Mistral, or Ollama) and understand the difference between system prompts, user prompts, and completion endpoints. They may not be familiar with ontological modeling or dependency graph theory, so the framework explains these concepts progressively through Series 1. The audience profile directly informs the verbosity level (moderate), abstraction level (mixed concrete/formal), and terminology choices (industry standard with definitions for novel terms) across the entire framework.

variants.architect: The audience segmentation reveals distinct interface requirements that should influence the system's layering. Practitioners (TypeScript developers) interact with the CLI in src/cli/ and need programmatic access to artifacts. Product managers interact via the web UI in web/ and need visual progress tracking and export capabilities. Architects need the full artifact dictionary and dependency graph visualization. The baseline familiarity assumption — that users understand REST APIs, npm, and LLM concepts — directly constrains the error handling strategy in src/engine/validator.ts: validation errors should reference question IDs and artifact keys, not internal state representations. The audience profile also shapes the context_template field in OpenEndedQuestion: templates should assume knowledge of basic software engineering but explain SPACE-specific concepts like 'artifact dictionary' and 'series dependency' inline. The secondary audiences (maintainers, technical writers) consume exported artifacts, not the elicitation engine itself, which justifies the clean separation between src/engine/ (internal) and src/export/ (external consumption).
variants.practitioner: The practitioner needs to understand the full data flow: Framework JSON → FrameworkLoader → QuestionRouter → SessionManager → ArtifactExtractor → ArtifactDictionary → ExportCompiler → ExportResult. The ArtifactExtractor (src/data/artifact-extractor.ts) has series-specific extraction patterns for all 7 series, with transformers that parse free-text answers using regex patterns and keyword detection. Each extraction includes confidence estimation based on answer length, structure, and source count. The ArtifactTracker (src/data/artifact-tracker.ts) provides content hashing (SHA-256 truncated to 12 chars) for change detection, staleness detection when upstream answers change, and what-if analysis for exploring answer change impacts. Configuration is now validated at startup via assertValidConfig() — if you pass an invalid llm_provider, it throws immediately rather than falling through to NullProvider silently. Environment variables are wired via configFromEnv() which maps SPACE_PROJECTS_DIR, SPACE_LLM_PROVIDER, SPACE_LLM_API_KEY, etc.

The technical writer audience is the fastest path to viral adoption: if SPACE specs become the input format for documentation generators (Docusaurus, GitBook, ReadMe), each technical writer who adopts SPACE creates a multiplier effect. The roadmap should prioritize: (1) CLI for developers (MVP, months 1-3), (2) Web UI for PMs (months 4-6), (3) Export integration with doc platforms (months 7-9). text: What foundational concepts, theorems, or prior art can the output take for granted? What must be explained from scratch?

choices.text: Full prerequisites assumed — dive straight into advanced material
Core fundamentals assumed; edge cases and advanced topics explained
First-principles treatment — no prior knowledge assumed

answer:
Assumed knowledge that the output can take for granted: CLI tool usage (npm install, git clone, running scripts), Node.js/TypeScript basics (import/export, async/await, type annotations, interfaces), JSON/YAML parsing and structure, REST API concepts (endpoints, request/response, status codes), prompt engineering fundamentals (system prompts, few-shot prompting, temperature, top_p), and basic software architecture patterns (MVC, event-driven, plugin systems, dependency injection).

Must be explained from scratch: (1) The specific 7-series progressive elicitation methodology — how questions build on each other across series in a dependency graph. (2) The dependency chain between series — why Series 2 (Ontological Characteristics) cannot start until Series 1 (Conceptual Depth) provides domain and audience context, and why Series 7 (Operational/Functional) depends on both Series 5 and 6. (3) How artifacts accumulate — each answer contributes extracted data (entity lists, relationship graphs, procedure steps, tech stack decisions) that downstream series consume via the artifact dictionary. (4) The 326-probe structure — 67 open-ended questions, each with 3-5 multi-choice follow-ups that classify and clarify the answer, totaling 201+ follow-up choices. (5) How the framework produces a coherent specification from apparently disconnected questions through the artifact dependency graph. (6) The StorageProvider abstraction — how sessions persist via filesystem or SQLite. (7) The LLM provider factory — how multiple AI backends (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Ollama) are abstracted behind a unified interface.

variants.architect: SPACE can take for granted foundational software engineering concepts: module systems, async control flow, type systems, and data serialization. The output can assume familiarity with the TypeScript ecosystem (interfaces, generics, union types) since the entire codebase is TypeScript. However, several concepts must be introduced from scratch: the FrameworkDefinition structure (the 7-series hierarchy is SPACE-specific), the ArtifactDictionary pattern (a dynamic key-value store where keys are semantically meaningful and values carry provenance metadata), and the dependency graph model (how series consume artifacts from predecessor series). The JAD facilitation model should be referenced but not assumed — the system's progressive questioning approach borrows from JAD but operates differently. The OWL-style ontological modeling reference is aspirational; the system extracts entity definitions from free-text answers but does not implement formal reasoning. What must be explained from scratch: the concept of a 'probe' (a structured question designed to elicit specific information), the 'artifact' as a living document that evolves across series, and the snapshot mechanism for preserving intermediate state.
variants.practitioner: The prior art SPACE can leverage includes: dependency graph implementations (topological sort in src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts), state machine patterns for session lifecycle (created → in_progress → completed), and repository pattern for storage (src/storage/types.ts defines the StorageProvider interface). The practitioner should reference existing TypeScript patterns: discriminated unions for SpaceEvent types (already in types/index.ts), branded types for session/project IDs, and the builder pattern for ExportOptions. Concepts requiring explanation from scratch: the context_template interpolation system (how question text adapts based on prior artifacts), the artifact confidence scoring (0.0-1.0 scale in ArtifactValue), and the quality scoring dimensions in src/llm/quality-scorer.ts (completeness, specificity, consistency, actionability). The completeness-scorer in src/intelligence/ implements a custom scoring algorithm that doesn't follow standard heuristics — this needs API docs. The snapshot-manager.ts creates periodic checkpoints during sessions, which is an uncommon pattern in CLI tools that practitioners may not expect.

SPACE differentiates by being specification-focused rather than content-focused. The concepts it must explain from scratch (probe-based elicitation, artifact dictionaries, series dependencies) are its unique value props and competitive moat — these are the innovations that justify a standalone tool rather than a ChatGPT plugin. The risk is that explaining these concepts requires significant documentation investment. The strategy should be: invest heavily in the first-session experience (guided walkthrough with pre-filled example answers) so users learn by doing rather than reading. text: At what level of abstraction should the output operate? Should it be concrete and example-driven, or formal and general?

choices.text: Concrete — specific examples, code snippets, case studies
Mixed — conceptual frameworks illustrated with examples
Formal — definitions, proofs, mathematical notation, first-order logic

answer:
Mixed approach — present the SPACE architecture with clear structural diagrams showing the series dependency graph and question flow, then ground each concept with concrete examples from the actual codebase.

For the structural layer: use dependency graphs (Series 1 feeds Series 2, which feeds Series 3; Series 2+3 feed Series 4; Series 1+4 feed Series 5; Series 4+5 feed Series 6; Series 5+6 feed Series 7) to show the progressive narrowing. Show how each series consumes artifacts from previous series via the artifact dictionary. Show the series/round/question hierarchy with the z_multi_choice_per_open parameter controlling follow-up depth.

For the concrete layer: show actual TypeScript code snippets from the engine (question-router.ts showing dependency resolution, session-manager.ts showing state transitions, artifact-mapping.ts showing extraction patterns), real JSON examples of session state (with question answers, artifact dictionaries, and completion flags), and actual output from the export pipeline (JSON spec, Markdown doc, YAML config, HTML report, LLM prompt). The abstraction level balances formal definitions (the StorageProvider interface, the LLMProvider interface, the SpaceConfig type) with illustrative examples (actual terminal output from "space run", actual JSON artifact entries).

variants.architect: The mixed abstraction approach is architecturally sound because SPACE operates at multiple levels simultaneously: the question framework (abstract, declarative), the engine (concrete, imperative), and the LLM integration (probabilistic, contextual). Presenting the dependency graph as a structural diagram first grounds the reader in the system's topology, then concrete code examples from src/engine/question-router.ts demonstrate how the abstract graph is traversed at runtime. The key architectural insight is that the system has two distinct abstraction layers: (1) the framework definition layer (JSON files, immutable, purely declarative) and (2) the session/execution layer (TypeScript runtime, mutable state, imperative logic). The abstraction level should shift as the document progresses: Series 1 answers establish conceptual grounding (abstract), Series 2-3 build the entity model (semi-formal), and Series 4-7 specify implementation details (concrete). This mirrors the actual codebase structure where src/types/ is abstract, src/engine/ is semi-abstract, and src/cli/ is concrete.
variants.practitioner: The concrete examples should ground each concept in actual code paths. For example, when explaining the dependency graph, show how src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts implements topological sort over the DependencyGraph type from src/types/index.ts. When explaining artifact extraction, show how src/data/artifact-mapping.ts transforms free-text AnswerEntry values into structured ArtifactValue objects. The session lifecycle can be demonstrated by walking through src/engine/session-manager.ts: session.create() → session.submitAnswer() → session.nextQuestion() → session.export(). Each code example should include the function signature, a brief usage pattern, and the relevant type contract. The engine's core loop (in src/engine/core.ts) is the most concrete demonstration: it shows how the system moves from question to question, checks dependencies, extracts artifacts, and tracks progress. Concrete error handling examples should reference src/engine/validator.ts patterns like ValidationResult and the error code conventions used in SpaceEvent.
variants.strategist: The abstraction level decision directly impacts developer adoption speed. If SPACE starts too abstract (methodology-first), developers will lose interest before seeing working code. If it starts too concrete (install-and-run), they won't understand the 326-probe framework's value. The recommended approach for the web audience: lead with the output (a sample specification generated by SPACE) then work backward to the methodology. For the CLI audience: lead with the command (npx space init) and let the progressive questioning demonstrate the methodology in practice. The strategic document should maintain two parallel tracks: a 'quick start' (concrete, 5 minutes to first spec) and a 'deep dive' (abstract, comprehensive architecture explanation). Market data suggests developer tools with both tracks see 3x higher conversion than tools that only offer one. text: What vocabulary, jargon, or notation should be used or deliberately avoided? Are there established standards the output should follow?

choices.text: Standard industry terminology — use common terms precisely
Plain accessible language — minimize jargon; explain what is used
Formal academic register — precise definitions, technical notation

answer:
Standard software engineering terminology used consistently throughout: session (a user interaction instance with a unique UUID), artifact (extracted structured data from answers, stored in the artifact dictionary), framework (the 326-probe question set defined in JSON), series (a themed group of rounds, 7 total), round (a batch of 2-5 related open-ended questions), probe (a single elicitation question — open-ended or multi-choice follow-up), dependency (a series that must complete before another can start).

Industry terms used precisely: dependency injection (for the StorageProvider pattern allowing filesystem or SQLite backends), factory pattern (for LLM provider creation via createLLMProvider()), event emitter (for lifecycle hooks in the session manager), command pattern (for CLI commands in src/cli/commands/), strategy pattern (for export format selection), adapter pattern (for the StorageProvider implementations).

Terms deliberately avoided: "AI" or "intelligent" for the engine (it routes and extracts deterministically, not "understands"), "user" for the respondent (use "respondent" or "answerer" to distinguish from system operators), "generate" for the export (use "compile" or "render" to distinguish from LLM generation), "smart" for any feature (avoid marketing language in technical specifications), "revolutionary" or "groundbreaking" for the methodology (it's a practical engineering tool, not a research paper).

Notation conventions: question IDs use dot notation (e.g., "2.3.1" = Series 2, Round 3, Question 1). Artifact keys use snake_case (e.g., "entity_list", "relationship_graph"). File paths use forward slashes. Code references use backtick formatting.

variants.architect: SPACE establishes a domain-specific vocabulary that must be used with absolute consistency across all interfaces — CLI output, web UI, exported specs, and documentation. Key terms that carry architectural significance: 'session' (a bounded execution context, not a user session), 'artifact' (derived structured data, not a build artifact), 'series' (a question group, not a data series), 'round' (a progressive step within a series), 'probe' (an elicitation question, not a network probe). The vocabulary follows the Adapter pattern — mapping general concepts to SPACE-specific terms. The notation conventions should follow JSON Schema patterns for the framework definition files and TypeScript conventions for the codebase. Terms to deliberately avoid: 'prompt' (confusing with LLM prompts — SPACE uses 'question' or 'probe'), 'model' (confusing with ML models — SPACE uses 'framework' or 'entity'), 'template' (confusing with HTML templates — SPACE uses 'context_template' for the specific field). The established standard is: all SPACE-specific terms are lowercase with underscores (snake_case), matching the JSON framework file convention.
variants.practitioner: In the codebase, terminology is enforced through TypeScript types in src/types/index.ts. The interface names serve as vocabulary anchors: SessionState, ArtifactDictionary, FrameworkDefinition, QuestionContext. When implementing new features, developers must use these exact type names — not synonyms. The src/cli/tui.ts and web/ should display the same terminology to users. For example, the CLI shows 'Series 2: Ontological Characteristics' and the web UI must show the identical label. The artifact key naming convention (e.g., 'entity_list', 'domain_scope', 'tech_stack') should be documented in src/data/artifact-mapping.ts with JSDoc comments explaining each key's semantic meaning. When writing tests, test descriptions should use the canonical terminology: 'should complete round when all questions answered' not 'should finish step when all prompts done.' The context_template interpolation system uses {{artifact_key}} placeholders that reference the artifact dictionary — the syntax is Mustache-style (double curly braces) and should not be confused with TypeScript template literals.
variants.strategist: The terminology choice directly impacts SEO, community building, and market positioning. 'Probe' is more distinctive than 'question' and creates a unique search identity — when users search 'SPACE probes' or 'elicitation probes,' the tool owns that keyword space. 'Artifact' is problematic because it collides with Maven/Gradle build artifacts in developer search results. Consider 'spec artifact' or 'design artifact' as a compound term to differentiate. The vocabulary decisions should be finalized before any public documentation is published — changing terminology after launch creates migration pain and community confusion. The established standards alignment matters for integration: if SPACE artifacts follow JSON Schema conventions, they can be consumed by tools like Postman, Swagger, and OpenAPI generators, which expands the addressable market. The deliberate avoidance of 'prompt' is strategically important — it positions SPACE as distinct from prompt engineering tools, which is correct because SPACE is a specification tool that happens to use LLMs, not a prompt engineering tool that happens to generate specs.

answer:
Progressive scaffolding — start with the simple concept of asking structured questions to produce specifications, then layer in complexity one dimension at a time:

Layer 1 (Series 1): Question asking — the basic loop of presenting questions and recording answers. Establish domain, audience, vocabulary, and abstraction level. This is the simplest concept and requires no prerequisite knowledge.

Layer 2 (Series 2): Entity discovery — identify the primary entities, attributes, categories, and boundaries of the domain. Introduce the concept of ontological modeling (but call it "entity mapping" for accessibility). Show how free-text answers are parsed for entity mentions.

Layer 3 (Series 3): Relationship mapping — connect entities with associations, hierarchies, causal chains, and dependencies. Introduce graph theory concepts (nodes, edges, directed graphs) through concrete examples.

Layer 4 (Series 4): Procedural scoping — define workflows, decision points, error handling, and step granularity. Connect procedures to entities (procedures operate on entities) and relationships (procedures traverse relationships).

Layer 5 (Series 5): Technical specifications — hardware, software, performance, security, integrations, and timeline. This is the most concrete layer and grounds all previous abstract concepts in specific technology choices.

Layer 6 (Series 6): Development methodology — team process, quality practices, communication patterns. Connects technical specifications to human organization.

Layer 7 (Series 7): Operational preferences — deployment, monitoring, maintenance, stewardship. The final layer that ensures the specification is actionable.

Each layer builds on all previous layers. The complexity distribution is deliberately front-loaded: Series 1-2 introduce the most new concepts, Series 3-4 apply them, Series 5-7 ground them in specifics. This matches the progressive disclosure pattern where users learn the framework by doing, not by reading documentation.

variants.architect: The progressive complexity distribution follows the Layered Architecture pattern, where each layer builds on the previous one's abstractions. Layer 1 (Series 1) establishes the vocabulary and basic data model — FrameworkDefinition, SessionState. Layer 2 (Series 2-3) introduces the artifact extraction pipeline and dependency resolution. Layer 3 (Series 4-5) adds LLM integration and quality scoring. Layer 4 (Series 6-7) specifies export formats and deployment. This layering maps directly to the src/ directory structure: types/ → engine/ → llm/ → export/. The architectural benefit is that each layer can be understood, tested, and modified independently. The risk of this approach is that users who only complete Series 1-2 will have an incomplete mental model of the system's full capabilities. The mitigation is that each series' output (exported specification) should be independently useful, not just a stepping stone to the full specification.

In src/engine/core.ts, the core loop starts with the simplest case: load framework → display question → collect answer → extract artifacts → route to next question. The implementation should follow this same progressive pattern in tests: first test the basic question-answer loop, then add dependency resolution, then add artifact extraction, then add LLM refinement. The context_template field on each OpenEndedQuestion drives this progressive revelation — earlier questions have no context_template, later ones interpolate prior artifacts.

answer:
Core entities identified through systematic domain analysis of the SPACE system:

1. Framework — The 326-probe question set. Contains 7 series, each with multiple rounds, each round with 2-5 open-ended questions, each question with 3-5 multi-choice follow-ups. Defined in JSON files under prompt-framework/json/. Immutable after creation; the framework is the reference specification.

2. Series — A themed group of rounds within the framework. 7 series total: Conceptual Depth, Ontological Characteristics, Semantic Relationships, Procedural Breadth, Technical Specifications, Development Methodologies, Operational/Functional. Each series has dependencies (other series that must complete first), consumes (artifacts it needs), and provides (artifacts it produces).

3. Round — A batch of related open-ended questions within a series. Each round has a focus area (e.g., "Entity Discovery", "System Boundaries") and contains 2-5 questions that share thematic coherence.

4. Question — A single elicitation probe. Two types: open-ended (free text response) and multi-choice follow-up (classify the open-ended answer). Each question has a unique ID (e.g., "2.3.1"), text (the question prompt), and follow_up_choices (2-5 options).

5. Answer — A respondent's response to a question. Contains the open-ended text (the free response) and the chosen follow-up option (the classification). Answers are stored in session state.

6. Artifact — Structured data extracted from answers. Created by the artifact mapping system which parses free-text answers for entity mentions, architectural decisions, technology choices, and constraints. Artifacts accumulate across series and are consumed by downstream series.

7. Session — A complete interaction instance. Has a UUID, project association, current question pointer, answer history, artifact dictionary, and completion status. Sessions can be resumed from storage.

8. Project — A named workspace. Contains sessions, exports, and configuration. Stored in ~/.space/projects/<name>/.

9. Export — A compiled specification document. Multiple formats: JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML, LLM prompt. Generated on-demand from session state and artifact dictionary.

10. Engine — The orchestration layer. Manages question routing, answer validation, artifact extraction, and session lifecycle. The core runtime that ties everything together.

variants.architect: The entity model has 10 types: Framework, Series, Round, Question, Choice, Answer, Artifact, Session, Project, Export. The deliberate choice of no inheritance (standalone interfaces in src/types/index.ts) reduces complexity but introduces some code duplication. The ArtifactExtractor service (src/data/artifact-extractor.ts) is now a separate concern from SessionManager, with extraction patterns registered per series. The ArtifactTracker (src/data/artifact-tracker.ts) provides version tracking and staleness detection — when a user re-answers a question, the tracker can identify which downstream artifacts are now stale. The ArtifactDictionary type uses Record<string, ArtifactValue> with no schema enforcement at the type level, but the new validateArtifactDictionary() function catches unknown keys at extraction time using the KNOWN_ARTIFACT_KEYS set. The main architectural risk remains that ArtifactValue.value is typed as 'any' — a full Zod schema would catch more issues but adds runtime overhead.
variants.practitioner: The entity list maps to TypeScript interfaces in src/types/index.ts. FrameworkDefinition → Framework, SeriesDefinition → Series, RoundDefinition → Round, OpenEndedQuestion → Question, MultiChoice → Choice. These are the 'definition' types (static, loaded from JSON). SessionMeta, AnswerEntry, ArtifactValue, ProgressState are the 'runtime' types (mutable, persisted to storage). The src/data/framework-loader.ts reads JSON files and produces FrameworkDefinition objects. The src/engine/question-router.ts traverses the framework's series/round/question hierarchy using the SeriesDefinition.rounds array. The src/data/artifact-mapping.ts defines the mapping between question IDs and artifact keys — this is the critical bridge between the definition layer and the runtime layer. When implementing new entity types, check if they belong in the definition layer (add to FrameworkDefinition side) or the runtime layer (add to SessionState side). The storage layer (src/storage/types.ts) defines how entities are serialized to SQLite or filesystem.
variants.strategist: The entity model is the foundation for all product features. The Framework entity (the 326-question structure) is the primary intellectual property — it encodes the methodology that differentiates SPACE. The Session entity represents the user's work product — completed sessions are the output users value and share. The ArtifactDictionary is the bridge between input (answers) and output (specifications) — it's where AI augmentation adds the most value through extraction and refinement. The Project entity supports team use cases (multiple sessions for the same project, compare-and-merge workflows) that justify paid tiers. Product roadmap should prioritize: (1) Framework authoring tools (let users customize the 326 probes), (2) Session sharing (let team members see each other's answers), (3) Artifact visualization (entity relationship diagrams from the artifact dictionary). The entity model's clean separation between definition and runtime enables a marketplace where users can author and share custom frameworks — a significant revenue opportunity.
variants.ethicist: From an ethical standpoint, entity modeling carries significant implications for fairness and representation. The act of categorizing entities — deciding what is 'core' versus 'peripheral' — embeds value judgments about what matters in the system. When we define entity attributes, we are essentially encoding a worldview: which properties are visible, which are hidden, and which are deemed irrelevant. The cardinality relationships between entities reflect power structures — one-to-many patterns can encode hierarchical oppression if the 'one' represents institutional authority and the 'many' represent individuals. The system boundary question is particularly fraught: defining what is 'in scope' versus 'out of scope' determines whose concerns are heard and whose are excluded. Environmental impact also matters — the JSON-file storage model is energy-efficient compared to database-backed systems, but the LLM integration introduces carbon costs through API calls to cloud inference clusters.
variants.futurist: Entity modeling is undergoing a paradigm shift from static schemas to dynamic, AI-interpreted ontologies. Within 3-5 years, the manual entity discovery process will be augmented by LLMs that can infer entity types, attributes, and relationships from natural language descriptions — reducing the 15-question Series 2 to 3-5 targeted validation prompts. The classification schemes we use today (core vs. peripheral, functional role, data lifecycle) will be replaced by embedding-based similarity clustering where entities are grouped by semantic proximity rather than explicit categories. The cardinality relationships will evolve from fixed schemas (one-to-many, many-to-many) to probabilistic relationships expressed as confidence scores. The entity lifecycle management will shift from manual state machines to event-sourced systems where entity state is derived from a log of all changes. By 2030, the concept of a 'static entity model' will feel as antiquated as manual memory management feels today.
variants.educator: Teaching entity modeling requires hands-on practice with concrete examples before abstract principles. The recommended learning sequence is: (1) Study the existing entity definitions in src/types/index.ts to understand the type system, (2) Walk through a complete Series 2 session using the web UI, (3) Examine the artifact-mapping.ts file to see how free-text answers become structured entity data, (4) Practice defining entities for a familiar domain (e.g., a library catalog or restaurant menu). The classroom exercise should have students model the entities of their own project, then compare with peers to identify gaps. The key pedagogical insight is that entity modeling is an iterative process — the first pass is always incomplete, and the refinement rounds (Series 2, Rounds 4-5) teach students to revisit and improve their initial models. Assessment should evaluate not just completeness but also the quality of entity relationships and the appropriateness of granularity choices.

answer:
Three natural categories emerge from functional analysis:

Category 1 — Structural Entities (define the system's shape): Framework, Series, Round, Question. These are the static definition entities that don't change during a session. They define WHAT gets asked and in what order. The dependency graph lives here — Series dependencies create a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that determines execution order.

Category 2 — Runtime Entities (capture the session's state): Session, Answer, Artifact. These are the dynamic entities that change as the session progresses. They capture WHAT was answered and what was extracted. The artifact dictionary is the central data structure here — it accumulates across all series.

Category 3 — Output Entities (produce the deliverables): Project, Export, Engine. These are the container and delivery entities. Projects hold sessions, Exports hold compiled specifications, and the Engine orchestrates everything.

The categories map to architectural layers: structural → data model (JSON schema definitions), runtime → engine layer (session management, artifact extraction), output → export layer (format compilation, file I/O). The dependency graph creates cross-category relationships where structural entities (Series) consume output entities (Artifacts) from other structural entities — this is the key insight that makes the framework self-referential.

The category boundaries are clean: no entity belongs to multiple categories. This separation enables independent testing (structural entities can be validated without runtime entities) and independent evolution (adding a new export format doesn't affect structural entities).

Core entities (system cannot function without): Framework, Session, Question, Artifact, Engine. These five entities are the minimal viable set — without any one of them, the system cannot ask questions, record answers, or produce output.

Framework defines what to ask. Question defines individual probes. Session captures the interaction. Artifact extracts structured data. Engine orchestrates the flow.

Answer is the data record of a Question response — without it, the system would lose history, but the extraction could theoretically happen in real-time. Project is a container — without it, sessions would be unorganized but still functional. Export is a deliverable — without it, the system produces artifacts but no compiled specifications.

The core/peripheral split is important for implementation: core entities get first-class type definitions, comprehensive validation, and priority error handling. Peripheral entities get simpler types and can tolerate graceful degradation (e.g., if Export generation fails, the session data is still preserved).

The Project becomes core if multi-project management is a requirement (which it currently is). This context-dependency is why the entity model includes both perspectives.

text: At what level of granularity should entities be modeled? Should fine distinctions be separate entities or attributes of coarser ones?

choices.text: Coarse-grained — entities are broad; most variation is captured via attributes
Moderate — key specializations become distinct entities
Fine-grained — every meaningful distinction yields a separate entity

answer:
Moderate granularity — key specializations become distinct entities, but trivial variations are collapsed.

Example of appropriate splitting: Session and Answer are separate entities even though Answers live inside Sessions, because Answers have their own lifecycle (they can be edited, skipped, or marked as invalid) and their own relationships (each Answer links to exactly one Question and contributes to specific Artifacts).

Example of appropriate merging: Round and Focus are NOT separate entities. The "focus" is just a string attribute of Round. Splitting them would add complexity without enabling new behaviors.

Example of progressive refinement: The initial model had separate "OpenEndedAnswer" and "MultiChoiceAnswer" entities. These were merged into a single "Answer" entity with a choice_id attribute that may be null (for open-ended only) or populated (for follow-up classification). The split wasn't adding value because both types share the same lifecycle and storage.

Granularity decision criteria: An entity should be separate if it (a) has a distinct lifecycle, (b) participates in unique relationships, (c) has attributes not shared with the candidate parent, or (d) is independently addressable (has its own ID). Question passes all four tests. Round passes tests (a) and (d) but not (b) and (c) — yet it's still separate because it provides essential organizational structure.

The balance: 10 entity types total. Fine enough to capture all meaningful distinctions in the system. Coarse enough to keep the type system manageable. Each entity has 5-15 attributes. The total attribute count across all entities is approximately 80, which is within the cognitive load limit for a single developer.

text: How do entities relate to each other in terms of sharing, inheriting, or differentiating attributes?

choices.text: Mostly independent — entities share few attributes beyond common identifiers
Shared attributes grouped by category — entities in same category share a profile
Inheritance hierarchy — subtypes inherit and extend parent attributes
Mixin / trait composition — entities compose attribute sets from multiple sources
Dynamic — attribute sharing depends on entity state or context

answer:
Shared attributes grouped by functional category:

Universal attributes (shared by most entities): id (unique identifier), created_at (timestamp), updated_at (timestamp). These are present on Session, Answer, Artifact, Project, and Export. Question and Framework use id but not timestamps (they're static definitions).

Structural attributes (shared by definition entities): name, description, text. Framework has name+description. Series has name+description. Round has focus. Question has text. These are all human-readable strings that describe the entity's purpose.

Relational attributes (shared by entities that reference others): The FK pattern appears on Session (project_id → Project), Answer (question_id → Question), Artifact (source_question_id → Question), Export (session_id → Session). The consistency of this pattern (always string FKs, always referencing by ID) simplifies the storage layer.

Content attributes (unique to each entity): Framework has depends_on/provides/consumes arrays. Session has answers/artifacts dictionaries. Answer has open_ended/choice_id. Artifact has key/value/confidence. These are the distinguishing attributes that make each entity type necessary.

The dependency graph between Series creates a cross-cutting concern: Series entities have both structural attributes (name, description, rounds) and dependency attributes (deps, consumes, provides). The consumes/provides arrays use string keys that must match artifact dictionary keys — this implicit contract is enforced at runtime by the question router, not at compile time. A type-safe artifact key type could improve this.

variants.architect: Entity relationships follow three patterns: composition (Framework owns Series, Series owns Round), reference (Answer references Question, Artifact references Question), and aggregation (Project contains Sessions). The shared attributes (id, created_at, updated_at) are universal value object fields that could be extracted into a base type. The differentiation follows the Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) model for ArtifactValue, where the value attribute can hold any type and the key provides semantic meaning. Inheritance is minimal — there's no type hierarchy among entities, which is a deliberate design choice to keep the model flat and simple. The relationship between Framework entities (definition) and Session entities (runtime) is the most architecturally significant: they share the same keys (question IDs, series numbers) but have different lifecycles and storage strategies. This is the Foreign Key pattern where Answer.question_id references Question.id across the definition/runtime boundary.
variants.practitioner: Shared attributes are implemented as base interfaces that concrete entities extend. The id field is typed as string (UUID for runtime entities, hierarchical string like '1.1.1' for definition entities). The created_at/updated_at fields use ISO 8601 strings (not Date objects) for serialization compatibility — this is enforced in src/types/index.ts. The relationship between Answer and Question is maintained by the question_id field in AnswerEntry, which must match a valid question ID in the framework definition. The src/engine/validator.ts checks this referential integrity when answers are submitted. The ArtifactValue.source_question_id provides the reverse reference — tracing artifacts back to their source questions. The src/data/artifact-mapping.ts defines the mapping between question IDs and artifact keys, which is the schema for the reference relationship. When implementing cross-referencing features, use the question ID as the canonical join key between definition and runtime entities.

text: What are the systemic boundaries of this domain? What is explicitly in scope vs. out of scope?

choices.text: Tightly bounded — scope is narrow and well-defined
Moderately bounded — clear core with some fuzzy edges
Loosely bounded — domain bleeds into adjacent areas
Bounded by role/perspective — different stakeholders draw different boundaries

answer:
Tightly bounded — scope is narrow and well-defined.

The system boundary encompasses: the CLI interface (src/cli/), the core engine (src/engine/), the storage layer (src/storage/), the LLM integration (src/llm/), the export pipeline (src/export/), the web UI (web/), and the test suite (tests/).

Outside the boundary: external LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral), the user's filesystem (projects directory), and the npm registry (for distribution). The system interacts with these through well-defined interfaces (HTTP for LLM APIs, filesystem API for storage, npm CLI for distribution).

The boundary is enforced by: the StorageProvider interface (abstracts filesystem access), the LLMProvider interface (abstracts API calls), and the SpaceConfig type (defines all configurable parameters). No entity inside the boundary reaches outside except through these interfaces.

The tight boundary is a design strength: it makes the system predictable (limited external dependencies), testable (all interfaces can be mocked), and composable (users can integrate SPACE into larger workflows by calling createSpace() programmatically). The system can run fully offline (LLM integration is optional) and has no runtime dependencies beyond Node.js.

text: What external entities, systems, or actors interact with this domain but are not part of it?

choices.text: No external interactions — fully self-contained domain
1–3 external actors (users, upstream data sources, downstream consumers)
4–7 external actors with distinct interaction patterns
8+ external actors — the domain is a hub in a larger ecosystem

answer:
Three external actors with distinct interaction patterns:

1. Human Respondent — Primary actor. Interacts via CLI (terminal prompts) or Web UI (browser forms). Provides free-text answers to open-ended questions and selections from multi-choice follow-ups. The respondent's primary interaction loop: read question → formulate answer → type response → select classification → proceed to next question. The system must be responsive to this loop — no unnecessary friction, clear progress indication, ability to skip and return.

2. LLM API (Optional) — Secondary actor. Called when auto-fill is requested or when the respondent wants AI-assisted answer formulation. Interaction pattern: send question context + respondent's partial answer → receive suggested completion. The LLM is a tool, not a co-author — the respondent always has final say. Fallback: if LLM is unavailable, the system works identically without it.

3. File System / Browser Storage — Persistence actor. Sessions are saved as JSON files on disk (CLI) or in browser localStorage/IndexedDB (Web UI). The storage layer handles serialization, compression (for large sessions), and atomic writes (to prevent corruption). The system reads from storage on startup (resume session) and writes after each answer (checkpoint). No network storage, no cloud sync — purely local persistence.

No other actors interact with the system. There is no authentication, no multi-user support, no API server (the web UI serves static files + local REST API). The three-actor model keeps the system simple, secure, and offline-capable.

The Human Respondent interacts through the CLI (stdin/stdout) or Web UI (HTTP), providing free-text answers that the system cannot validate structurally (they're open-ended by design). The LLM Provider interacts through the LLMProvider interface (src/llm/types.ts), receiving completion/refinement requests and returning structured responses — this is an Adapter pattern that abstracts away provider-specific differences. The Storage Backend interacts through the StorageProvider interface (src/storage/types.ts), receiving CRUD operations and persisting state. The architectural boundary with each external actor is different: the Human boundary is user-interface (imprecise, needs validation), the LLM boundary is API (structured, needs error handling), and the Storage boundary is persistence (durable, needs transaction guarantees). The dependency-resolver in src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts is the internal component most affected by external actors because it must handle the case where LLM-based artifact extraction fails and fall back to user-provided answers.

text: What is the lifecycle of each entity? How are they created, modified, combined, retired?

choices.text: Simple lifecycle — create, read, update, delete (CRUD)
Stateful lifecycle — entities pass through defined states with transition rules
Versioned lifecycle — entities have history, revisions, or snapshots
Composite lifecycle — entities are assembled/disassembled from sub-entities
Evolving lifecycle — entities change type or role over time

answer:
Stateful lifecycle with well-defined transitions:

Session lifecycle: created → active → paused/completed. Created when "space init" or "space run" is invoked. Active while questions are being answered. Paused when the user exits (auto-saved). Completed when all questions are answered or skipped. Can be resumed from paused state.

Question lifecycle: presented → answered/skipped. Presented when the question router selects it (based on dependency resolution). Answered when the respondent provides both open-ended text and follow-up selection. Skipped when the respondent explicitly skips (with optional reason). Questions can be re-answered (overwriting previous answer).

Artifact lifecycle: extracted → refined → finalized. Extracted when an answer is processed (pattern matching, keyword detection). Refined when subsequent answers provide additional context. Finalized when the series completes (no more extraction possible for this artifact key).

Export lifecycle: not_generated → generated → stale. Generated on-demand when the user requests export. Stale when new answers have been recorded since the last export. Regeneration overwrites the stale export.

Entity lifecycle summary: Framework and Series are immutable (defined once, never change). Rounds and Questions are immutable (fixed in the framework JSON). Sessions are mutable (answers accumulate). Artifacts are mutable (refined across series). Exports are computed (regenerated from current state). The lifecycle model ensures data integrity: immutable entities provide a stable reference, mutable entities track progress, computed entities reflect current state.

variants.architect: Each entity follows a well-defined state machine pattern. Session: created → in_progress → completed/abandoned (managed by session-manager.ts). Artifact: extracted → refined → finalized (managed by artifact-synthesizer.ts). The lifecycle transitions are guarded by business rules: a Session can only transition from created to in_progress when the first question is answered; from in_progress to completed when all required questions are answered; from in_progress to abandoned when the user explicitly cancels. The Framework entity has no lifecycle — it's immutable and loaded once at startup. The Question entity has an implicit lifecycle within a session: available → displayed → answered → locked (once answered, the question cannot be re-answered without editing the session). The Snapshot entity is create-only (no updates or deletes) — it's a write-ahead log entry that preserves session state at specific checkpoints. The export lifecycle is: generated → delivered (written to disk or returned to caller).

The status field uses TypeScript string literal types for compile-time safety. The artifact lifecycle is implicit in src/llm/artifact-synthesizer.ts: extract() creates ArtifactValue from answer text, refine() updates the value with LLM-enhanced content, and the confidence score increases as the artifact matures. The snapshot lifecycle in src/engine/snapshot-manager.ts is simple: create() is called at round/series boundaries and on-demand via the manual trigger. Snapshots are immutable — they're never updated or deleted. The export lifecycle is stateless: generate() in each formatter produces an ExportResult that is immediately written to disk.

If most sessions are abandoned in Series 1 (methodology questions), the onboarding experience needs redesign. answer:
No merges or splits needed. The entity boundaries are clean and well-motivated.

Verification: Each entity passes the four-entity-test: (1) distinct lifecycle — yes for all 10 entities. (2) unique relationships — yes (no two entities have identical relationship patterns). (3) non-shared attributes — yes (each entity has at least 2 attributes not shared with any other entity). (4) independent addressability — yes (each entity has a unique ID).

The current 10-entity model is stable and should not change without significant new requirements. Entity changes are expensive: they cascade through the type system, storage schema, API contracts, test suite, and documentation. The cost-benefit ratio only favors changes when new features demand it.

One observation: the Answer entity currently stores both the open-ended text and the follow-up choice. An alternative design would split these into OpenEndedResponse and FollowUpResponse entities. This was considered and rejected because: (a) every question has both an open-ended and follow-up component (they're always co-created), (b) splitting adds a join requirement for any query that needs both, and (c) the lifecycle is identical (both created/updated together). The current unified Answer entity is the right design.

text: What constraints, invariants, or business rules apply to entity instances? What must always be true?

choices.text: Minimal constraints — entities have few invariants beyond uniqueness
Moderate constraints — several required fields and validity rules
Strict constraints — entities must satisfy complex invariants at all times
Context-dependent — constraints vary by entity state or relationship
Evolving — constraints will be discovered through usage patterns

answer:
Key constraints and invariants:

1. Framework Immutability — A Framework cannot be modified after creation. The JSON files are read-only at runtime. This ensures consistent question delivery across sessions.

2. Session Uniqueness — Each Session has a UUID that is unique across all projects. Generated via crypto.randomUUID(). No two sessions can share an ID.

3. Question ID Format — Question IDs follow the pattern "S.R.Q" where S=series (1-7), R=round (1-5), Q=question (1-5). This format is validated on load.

4. Dependency Ordering — A series cannot start until all its dependency series have completed at least one round. Enforced by the question router's dependency resolution algorithm.

5. Artifact Key Uniqueness — Each artifact key is unique within a session's artifact dictionary. Overwriting an existing key is allowed (refinement) but logged.

6. Answer Completeness — A question is considered "answered" only when both the open-ended text AND the follow-up choice are provided. Partial answers are stored but don't count toward completion.

7. Export Atomicity — Export generation is atomic — either all requested formats succeed or the operation fails cleanly. No partial exports are left on disk.

8. Storage Consistency — After each answer, the session state is written to disk atomically (write to temp file, then rename). This prevents corruption if the process is interrupted.

Runtime constraints (enforced during session execution): each Question can be answered at most once per Session, dependencies must be satisfied before a Series is unlocked, and the ArtifactDictionary must contain all required artifacts before export. These are enforced by src/engine/validator.ts. Data integrity constraints (enforced at storage time): Answer.question_id must reference a valid question, Artifact.source_question_id must reference a valid question, and Session.framework_version must match the loaded framework version. text: What edge cases, exceptions, or degenerate cases could break the entity model? How should they be handled?

choices.text: Few edge cases — the model is robust to real-world variation
Known edge cases — they are well-understood and can be handled explicitly
Many edge cases — the model needs to be flexible to accommodate them
Edge cases are domain-specific — they vary by deployment or context
Edge cases will emerge — the model should accommodate undefined unknowns

answer:
Edge cases and their handling:

1. Empty Session — User starts a session and immediately exits without answering any questions. Handling: session is saved with zero answers, zero artifacts, status "paused". Can be resumed or abandoned.

2. Duplicate Answers — User re-answers a question that was already answered. Handling: the new answer overwrites the old one. The artifact dictionary is re-extracted from the new answer. The old answer is lost (no version history in current implementation).

3. Very Long Answers — User provides an answer exceeding 5000 characters. Handling: the answer is stored in full. No truncation. The artifact extraction may be slower due to parsing but remains functional.

4. Invalid Follow-up Selection — User selects a follow-up choice that doesn't exist in the question's choices array. Handling: validation rejects the selection, returns an error, and re-presents the question.

5. Corrupted Session File — The session JSON file is manually edited or corrupted. Handling: the StorageProvider catches the parse error, logs a warning, and offers to start a new session. No crash.

6. Missing Framework Files — The prompt-framework JSON files are deleted or moved. Handling: the engine fails to load the framework and exits with a clear error message. No partial operation.

7. Concurrent Access — Two processes try to write to the same session file. Handling: not currently handled (single-user system). The last writer wins. This is acceptable for the current scope.

8. All Questions Skipped — If every question is skipped, the session completes with empty artifacts. The export produces a valid but empty specification. This is a valid edge case (user explored the framework without committing to answers).

variants.architect: The edge cases follow the robustness principle (be conservative in what you accept, liberal in what you send). Empty sessions are handled by allowing SessionMeta to exist with zero answers — the progress tracking calculates completion_pct as 0.0 and the export layer generates a skeleton specification with placeholder sections. Corrupted sessions are handled by the snapshot-manager.ts creating periodic checkpoints — if the current session state is corrupted, the most recent valid snapshot can be restored. Concurrent access is addressed by the single-writer model: only one process (CLI or web) modifies a session at a time, enforced by file locking in the filesystem backend. The dependency cycle edge case is prevented by the framework definition being a validated DAG — the dependency-resolver.ts performs a topological sort at startup and throws if a cycle is detected. The LLM failure edge case triggers a fallback to template-based artifact extraction (src/llm/providers/template-provider.ts).
variants.practitioner: The edge case handling is implemented across several modules. Empty session: session-manager.ts allows create() without any answers; progress.ts calculates 0% completion. Corrupted session: snapshot-manager.ts creates checkpoints at round/series boundaries; on session load, if the state is corrupted, the system offers to restore from the latest snapshot. File locking: the filesystem storage backend uses lockfile (or similar) to prevent concurrent writes. LLM failure: src/llm/factory.ts wraps provider creation in try/catch and falls back to template-provider. Framework validation: src/data/framework-loader.ts checks the dependency graph for cycles using Kahn's algorithm. Framework version mismatch: currently not validated (a gap) — adding a version check in the loader would prevent loading sessions created with incompatible framework versions. The error handling convention in src/engine/ uses the SpaceEvent error type with a code and message, where codes follow the pattern 'ERROR_CATEGORY_SPECIFIC'.
variants.strategist: Edge case handling directly impacts user trust and retention. text: What direct associations exist between entities? Which entities reference, point to, or are linked to which others?

choices.text: Sparse — fewer associations than entities; most entities are isolated
Moderate — roughly one association per entity on average
Dense — entities form a richly connected web

answer:
Direct associations between entities:

Framework → Series: containment (Framework "has" Series). Bidirectional: Series knows its parent Framework.
Series → Round: containment (Series "has" Rounds). Bidirectional.
Round → Question: containment (Round "has" Questions). Bidirectional.
Question → Choice: containment (Question "has" Choices). Unidirectional (Choices don't reference back).

Session → Answer: composition (Session "produces" Answers). Session owns Answers; Answers don't exist without Session.
Session → Artifact: composition (Session "extracts" Artifacts). Artifact dictionary is part of Session state.
Answer → Question: reference (Answer "responds to" Question). Weak reference — Answers can exist without their source Question (if framework changes).
Artifact → Question: reference (Artifact "derived from" Question). Traces provenance.
Export → Session: reference (Export "compiled from" Session). Weak reference.
Project → Session: composition (Project "contains" Sessions).

Association density: Moderate — 12 distinct associations across 10 entities. Most entities participate in 2-3 associations. The densest entity is Session (6 associations: contains Answers, contains Artifacts, belongs to Project, referenced by Exports, references current Question, tracks status).

The Framework subgraph (Framework → Series → Round → Question → Choice) forms a rigid directed tree where associations are exclusively parent-to-child containment. The Session subgraph (Project → Session → Answer/Artifact/Export) is a loose composition where the Session is the root aggregate. The bridge references (Answer→Question, Artifact→Question, Export→Session, Artifact→source_question_id) cross the boundary between these subgraphs as weak associations, which is architecturally sound — it means the two subgraphs can evolve independently. If you changed the Framework structure (adding Series 8, for example), existing Answers don't break because they reference questions by stable ID, not by tree position. The 12 associations across 10 entities yield an average of 1.2 edges per entity, which is moderate density. However, Session is a god aggregate with 6 associations — a potential sign that it's taking on too many responsibilities. Consider whether Artifact management should be extracted into a separate ArtifactStore or whether Export generation should be delegated to an ExportCompiler rather than living on Session.

The bidirectional containment (Series knows its parent Framework) is implemented by each child holding a `parentFrameworkId: string` — this is redundant with the parent holding the array, but it enables efficient lookups from child to parent without scanning the parent's array. In `src/engine/session-manager.ts`, the Session aggregate holds `answers: Map<string, Answer>` and `artifacts: Record<string, Artifact>`, making the composition relationship explicit. text: What is the nature or type of each association? Is it a use, creation, ownership, or communication link?

choices.text: Single type — all associations are of the same nature
2–3 distinct relationship types (e.g., owns, produces, references)
4–7 distinct relationship types covering different interaction modes

answer:
Association types and their semantics:

1. CONTAINS — Parent-to-child structural containment. Framework contains Series. Series contains Rounds. Round contains Questions. Question contains Choices. These are strong ownership relationships — deleting the parent deletes all children. Implementation: parent holds array of children.

2. REFERENCES — Weak linking between entities. Answer references Question (by question_id FK). Artifact references Question (by source_question_id FK). Export references Session (by session_id FK). These are weak relationships — deleting the referenced entity doesn't delete the referencing entity (but may leave orphaned references). Implementation: entity holds ID string of referenced entity.

3. PRODUCES — Creation relationship. Session produces Answers. Session produces Artifacts. These are stronger than references because the producing entity owns the created entity. Implementation: Session holds arrays/dictionaries of created entities.

4. CONSUMES — Data flow relationship. Series consumes Artifacts from previous Series. This is the most interesting association type because it creates the dependency graph. Implementation: Series defines "consumes" array of artifact keys; the question router checks that these artifacts exist before starting the series.

5. DEPENDS_ON — Ordering constraint between Series. Series A depends on Series B means A cannot start until B has completed. This is a weaker relationship than CONSUMES — it's about ordering, not data flow. Implementation: Series defines "deps" array of Series IDs.

Each type maps to a distinct implementation strategy, which means the code can use type-safe discriminated unions to handle relationships rather than resorting to runtime type checks. The CONTAINS/REFERENCES split is particularly important — it's the difference between an aggregate boundary (CONTAINS) and a cross-aggregate reference (REFERENCES) in Domain-Driven Design terms. Session's answers are contained (it owns them), while an Answer's reference to a Question crosses an aggregate boundary. This distinction drives the persistence strategy: CONTAINS entities are serialized together (Session file includes all Answers), while REFERENCES entities are resolved lazily by ID lookup. The CONSUMES type is the most novel — it creates a forward-only data flow where Series B can only read artifacts from Series A, never write to them. This is an architectural constraint that prevents circular dependencies and simplifies the dependency graph to a DAG. The DEPENDS_ON type is redundant with CONSUMES in most cases but provides an optimization: a Series can depend on another Series without consuming its artifacts (e.g., Series 7 depends on Series 5 but doesn't directly use its artifacts — it uses Series 6 artifacts that were derived from Series 5).

By 2027, the manual relationship mapping process will be replaced by AI-assisted graph construction where the human role shifts from mapping to validating.
variants.educator: Teaching relationship mapping builds on the entity modeling skills from Series 2. The prerequisite knowledge includes: understanding of graph theory basics (nodes, edges, directed graphs), familiarity with UML relationship notation, and experience with the SPACE entity model. The recommended pedagogical approach is example-driven: start with a simple domain (3-5 entities) and manually trace all relationships before using the framework. Common misconceptions include: confusing 'association' with 'dependency,' assuming all relationships are bidirectional, and over-specifying cardinality constraints. The classroom exercise should have students create a relationship graph on paper before entering answers into the system — this forces explicit thinking about connections. The educator should emphasize that relationship mapping is where the specification becomes actionable — entities without relationships are just a vocabulary list. Assessment criteria: completeness (all significant relationships captured), accuracy (cardinality and direction correct), and clarity (relationships are well-named and typed).

text: What parent-child, containment, or hierarchical relationships exist? Which entities are within, belong to, or are part of others?

choices.text: No hierarchy — all entities are peers with no containment structure
Shallow hierarchy (1–2 levels) — simple containment chains
Deep hierarchy (3+ levels) — multi-level nesting
DAG structured — entities form a directed acyclic graph with multiple parents

answer:
Hierarchy and containment structure:

The primary hierarchy is the Framework structure:
Framework (root)
  └── Series (7 children)
        └── Round (3-5 children per Series)
              └── Question (2-5 children per Round)
                    └── Choice (3-5 children per Question)

This is a strict tree hierarchy — no entity has multiple parents at the same level. Maximum depth: 4 levels (Framework → Series → Round → Question → Choice). Average branching factor: Series=7, Round=3.5, Question=3.5, Choice=3.5.

The runtime hierarchy is the Project structure:
Project (root)
  └── Session (0..N children)
        ├── Answer (0..326 children)
        ├── Artifact (0..~100 key-value pairs)
        └── Export (0..5 children)

The two hierarchies intersect at the Session level: a Session is both part of a Project hierarchy AND linked to a Framework hierarchy (through its current question pointer and answer references). This intersection is managed by the Engine, which translates between the static Framework hierarchy and the dynamic Session state.

variants.architect: SPACE implements two independent tree hierarchies that intersect at the Session level — a classic **two-hierarchy convergence pattern**. The Framework hierarchy is a static, immutable tree with maximum depth 4 (Framework → Series → Round → Question → Choice), and the Project hierarchy is a dynamic, mutable tree with depth 3 (Project → Session → Answer/Artifact/Export). The convergence point is Session, which belongs to the Project hierarchy at runtime but references Framework entities by ID for question navigation. This two-tree design is architecturally correct because the two hierarchies have different lifecycles: Framework trees are loaded once from JSON and never modified, while Project trees grow throughout the session. Merging them into a single hierarchy would create problems — you'd have Framework entities (which are definition-time) mixed with Session entities (which are runtime), violating the temporal separation principle. The 4-level depth is the maximum reasonable for a CLI tool — deeper nesting would make the question navigation UI unwieldy. The branching factor averaging 3.5 across all levels means the total entity count is roughly 7 × 3.5 × 3.5 × 3.5 ≈ 300, which maps closely to the 326 questions (the variance comes from non-uniform branching at the Round level). The DAG-structured alternative (multiple parents) was wisely rejected because it would complicate the progress tracking — if a Question belonged to multiple Rounds, you'd need a DAG-aware progress tracker rather than the simple linear one in `src/engine/progress.ts`.
variants.practitioner: The two hierarchies are implemented in separate code paths. The Framework hierarchy is loaded in `src/data/framework-loader.ts` as a nested object: `Framework { series: Series[] }` where `Series { rounds: Round[] }`, `Round { questions: Question[] }`, `Question { choices: Choice[] }`. This is a straightforward recursive structure — the loader reads JSON and the TypeScript types enforce nesting. The Project hierarchy lives in `src/engine/session-manager.ts` where `Project { sessions: Session[] }` and `Session { answers: Map<string, Answer>, artifacts: Record<string, Artifact>, exports: Export[] }`. The key implementation detail is that `Session.currentQuestionId: string` is the bridge between hierarchies — it points into the Framework tree by question ID, and the `src/engine/question-router.ts` uses this ID to navigate the Framework structure (find which Round, which Series, advance to next). The progress tracking in `src/engine/progress.ts` works on the Framework tree: it tracks which Questions have been answered by checking `session.answers.has(question.id)`. This is efficient because the check is O(1) per question. A practical concern: the `snapshot-manager.ts` serializes both hierarchies to disk. When resuming, it deserializes the Session hierarchy first, then re-loads the Framework from the original JSON file. If the Framework file was modified between sessions, question IDs might still match but the structural position could differ — the question-router needs to handle this gracefully by validating that the currentQuestionId still resolves to a valid position in the Framework tree.
variants.strategist: The two-hierarchy design is directly tied to SPACE's core value proposition: progressive specification building. The Framework hierarchy (4 levels deep) enables the user to see the big picture (7 Series) while working on the details (one Question at a time). The Project hierarchy (3 levels deep) enables resumability and versioning — a user can have multiple Sessions for the same Project, each producing different specifications. From a product perspective, the Framework hierarchy depth of 4 is ideal because it maps to the mental model developers already have: project → phases → steps → tasks. The 3-level Project hierarchy is simpler because users shouldn't need to think about Session internals — they just want to 'continue where I left off.' The DAG-structured alternative was correctly rejected because it would break the 'simple CLI experience' positioning: if users had to navigate a graph of Questions instead of a linear path, the tool would feel more like a database query builder than a specification engine.
