For the product roadmap, the two-hierarchy model supports a natural progression: v1 uses the CLI with both hierarchies fully functional, v2 adds a web UI that visualizes the Framework hierarchy as an interactive tree (users can jump between Series), v3 adds collaboration where multiple users can work on the same Project hierarchy simultaneously. The key metric is the progression rate: how many users complete all 7 Series? If the 4-level depth is causing drop-off, we can flatten to 3 levels by merging Rounds into Series.
variants.ethicist: The hierarchical structure of SPACE — Framework containing Series containing Rounds containing Questions containing Choices — has significant ethical implications for how knowledge is structured and imposed on users. The parent-child containment model embeds a specific epistemological worldview: that system requirements can be decomposed into a fixed tree of topics, and that each topic exists at exactly one level of abstraction. This is a form of gatekeeping. Users who approach specification-writing from a different cultural or disciplinary tradition — for instance, indigenous knowledge systems that emphasize circular or relational ontologies rather than hierarchical decomposition — may find the mandatory tree structure alienating. The Framework hierarchy is immutable, meaning no user can modify the structural assumptions baked into the tool. This creates a power asymmetry: the framework designers have permanently decided what categories exist, what their nesting relationships are, and which questions belong where. For enterprise deployments, the Project hierarchy introduces a different ethical concern: session data captures a developer's thinking process, revealing their knowledge gaps, biases, and strategic priorities. If session files are shared or stored on corporate infrastructure, this becomes surveillance data. The intersection point — where Session references Framework entities by ID — means that user behavior data is permanently linked to structural metadata, enabling granular profiling of individual cognitive patterns across sessions.
variants.futurist: The two-tree convergence pattern where Framework and Project hierarchies intersect at the Session level represents a transitional architecture. Within five years, the static JSON-defined Framework tree will likely give way to dynamically generated question structures powered by LLMs that adapt hierarchy depth and branching factor per-session based on the user's domain and prior answers. The fixed 4-level depth (Framework → Series → Round → Question → Choice) will look quaint as AI-native specification tools learn to flatten or deepen the hierarchy on the fly — asking fewer questions when the domain is simple, expanding into deeper nesting when complexity warrants it. The containment model itself will evolve: instead of strict parent-child trees, future specification frameworks will use graph-based knowledge structures where a single question can belong to multiple contextual neighborhoods simultaneously. The current architecture's separation of the static Framework tree from the dynamic Project tree is wise for today but will become unnecessary when both are generated and stored as vector embeddings in a knowledge graph. The session data currently serialized as JSON will shift to structured memory representations that LLMs can query directly, collapsing the distinction between human-authored framework structure and machine-generated specification artifacts.
variants.educator: Understanding SPACE's two hierarchies is essential before using the tool effectively. The Framework hierarchy (Framework → Series → Round → Question → Choice) is the question bank — it defines what you'll be asked and in what order. Think of it like a textbook's table of contents: the Framework is the book, Series are chapters, Rounds are sections, Questions are exercises, and Choices are the prompts you respond to. The Project hierarchy (Project → Session → Answer/Artifact/Export) is your work product — it's what you build as you go through the questions. A common beginner mistake is trying to skip ahead in the Framework hierarchy or wondering why they can't reorder Series. The answer is that the Framework is read-only and sequential by design — each Series builds on previous answers, so the order matters. The bridge between the two hierarchies is the Session's current question pointer, which always points into the Framework tree. For learners coming from database design backgrounds, note that this is NOT a relational model — there are no foreign keys or junction tables. The two trees are connected only through ID references in the Session object. If you're onboarding a team, start by explaining that the Framework is like a restaurant menu (fixed options in a fixed order) and the Project is like your meal (personal, accumulated over time, and exportable as a complete specification).

text: What inheritance, specialization, or generalization relationships exist? Which entities are kinds of other entities?

choices.text: No inheritance — each entity is unique in its type
Simple inheritance — a few parent types with child specializations
Polymorphic hierarchy — entities can serve as multiple types simultaneously
Trait-based — entities pick capabilities from a shared set of traits

answer:
Inheritance and specialization:

The entity model uses composition over inheritance. No entity inherits from another entity.

Why no inheritance: The 10 entities are distinct types with different attributes and behaviors. There is no "base entity" that others extend. Each entity has its own type definition in src/types/index.ts. The closest thing to inheritance is the StorageProvider interface — FileSystemStorage and SQLiteStorage both implement the same interface, but this is interface implementation, not entity inheritance.

Alternative considered: A "BaseEntity" abstract class with id, created_at, updated_at. Rejected because: (a) not all entities need timestamps (Framework, Series, Round, Question are static), (b) the id types differ (number for Framework/Series, string for Session/Answer/Artifact), (c) it would force uniform structure on heterogeneous entities.

Trait-based approach: Instead of inheritance, the system uses traits (behaviors) that entities opt into: "storable" (can be persisted), "extractable" (can have data extracted from it), "exportable" (can be compiled into output). These are not formal type system constructs but implementation patterns — a storable entity has a corresponding StorageProvider method, an extractable entity has an artifact extraction handler, an exportable entity has a format compiler.

variants.architect: SPACE uses composition over inheritance for its entity hierarchy, which is the correct choice for a data-driven system where entities are defined by their data, not their behavior. The absence of inheritance means the entity model is a flat type system — each entity type (Framework, Series, Round, Question, Choice, Session, Answer, Artifact, Export, Project) is a standalone interface with no shared base class or abstract parent. This simplifies serialization (no polymorphic deserialization needed) and testing (no virtual method dispatch to mock). The shared behavioral traits (timestamps, serialization, validation) are implemented via TypeScript mixins or utility functions rather than base classes, which is the modern TypeScript pattern. The implicit type hierarchy via the artifact type system is the one exception: artifact keys like 'entities', 'relationships', 'procedures' form an informal hierarchy where 'relationships' depends on 'entities' existing first. This hierarchy is enforced by the dependency resolver, not by type inheritance. The Series-specific specialization is actually configuration-driven: each Series has a `consumes` array and a `produces` array in its JSON definition, which defines what it needs and what it creates. This is dependency injection at the data level rather than specialization at the type level — Series 3 'specializes' in entity modeling not by subclassing a 'ModelingSeries' type, but by declaring that it consumes 'vision' artifacts and produces 'entities' artifacts.
variants.practitioner: The entity interfaces in `src/types/index.ts` use flat types with no inheritance. For example, `Series` and `Round` both have `id: string` and `name: string` properties, but these are independently declared rather than inherited from a common `Identifiable` base. This is the TypeScript convention for data transfer objects — you avoid base classes because they complicate JSON serialization (you need to handle prototype chains) and make type narrowing harder (TypeScript's type guard works best with flat types). The shared behaviors are implemented as standalone functions: `validateEntity(entity: unknown): entity is Series` in `src/engine/validator.ts`, `serializeToJSON(entity: Series | Round | Question): string` as a generic function. The Series-specific behavior (what it consumes, what it produces) is configured in the framework JSON files, not in TypeScript types. For example, in `src/data/artifact-mapping.ts`, the `ARTIFACT_DEFINITIONS` record maps artifact keys to their schemas — this is the closest thing to a 'type hierarchy' for artifacts, and it's entirely data-driven. To add a new artifact type, you add an entry to `ARTIFACT_DEFINITIONS` and update the relevant Series' `produces` array. No new TypeScript types needed. The practical implication: the artifact type system is extensible without code changes, which is important for community contributions (users can define custom artifact types by editing framework JSON).
variants.strategist: The composition-over-inheritance approach is strategically important for SPACE's extensibility story. In the developer tooling market, the most successful tools are the ones that let users extend behavior without modifying source code. By using data-driven Series configuration instead of TypeScript inheritance, SPACE allows framework authors to create new Series types (e.g., a 'Security Review' Series, a 'Performance Audit' Series) by editing JSON files rather than writing TypeScript. This is the same pattern that makes tools like ESLint (rule plugins), webpack (loaders/plugins), and Jekyll (generators) successful. The implicit type hierarchy via artifact keys is actually a feature, not a limitation — it means the artifact system can evolve without breaking existing frameworks. If you add a new artifact key 'security_findings', existing frameworks that don't reference it simply ignore it. From a product strategy perspective, the 'no inheritance' decision positions SPACE as a framework that users configure rather than extend with code. This is important for the target audience: developers who want to write specifications, not build tooling. The risk is that some power users will want to add custom behaviors (e.g., 'validate that all entities have descriptions') that require code changes. The mitigation is to build a plugin/extension system (which the architecture already hints at with the LLM provider abstraction in `src/llm/providers/`) that lets users add validation rules, artifact extractors, and export formats via configuration.
variants.ethicist: SPACE's deliberate use of composition over inheritance carries an ethical dimension that's easy to overlook. By refusing to let entity types inherit from one another, the system avoids encoding hierarchical assumptions about which concepts are 'more specific' versions of others. For example, if Question inherited from Entity, it would imply that Questions are a 'kind of' Entity with all its attributes — a subtle but important claim about what Questions fundamentally are. The flat entity model treats all 10 types as equally valid, distinct constructs with their own attributes. This is more equitable but also more honest: a Choice is not a 'specialized Question' and an Artifact is not a 'refined Answer.' The composition approach also has implications for accessibility. Because each entity type has its own explicit attributes rather than inheriting them from a parent class, the data model is more transparent — there are no hidden inherited fields that might confuse screen readers or debugging tools. However, the lack of a type hierarchy means there's no polymorphic processing: the system can't treat all 'output' entities the same way without explicit type checking. This means each new entity type requires dedicated handling code, which increases the surface area for bugs and the risk that edge cases for one entity type are overlooked while being handled for another.
variants.futurist: The rejection of inheritance in favor of composition is philosophically aligned with where software architecture is heading, but it will be insufficient within a decade. As specification tools converge with AI agents, the entity model will need to become polymorphic — but not through traditional OOP inheritance. Instead, expect behavioral interfaces defined by capability contracts: an entity that can be 'asked about' (Question-like), 'answered' (Answer-like), and 'exported' (Artifact-like) will compose these capabilities dynamically. The current 10 flat entity types will merge and split as the tool evolves: Question and Choice may become a single entity with a 'mode' flag, while Artifact and Export may gain shared rendering interfaces. Within five years, the entity model will likely shift to an event-sourced architecture where entities are projections of a stream of user interactions, not static typed objects. The composition-over-inheritance principle will survive but transform: instead of manual composition in TypeScript classes, it will manifest as composable plugin architectures where each entity type is a capability module that can be mixed into a runtime entity. The static type definitions in src/types/ will be replaced by runtime schema validation (Zod or similar) that allows dynamic entity types to be defined in JSON without recompilation.
variants.educator: SPACE uses composition over inheritance, which is a fancy way of saying: every entity type is its own thing with its own attributes, and no entity type is a 'child' or 'special case' of another. If you're coming from object-oriented programming, this might feel unusual — you might expect something like class Choice extends Question. Instead, each entity type (Framework, Series, Round, Question, Choice, Project, Session, Answer, Artifact, Export) has a completely independent type definition with its own fields. The practical benefit for learners is transparency: when you look at the TypeScript interfaces in src/types/, you can see exactly what attributes each entity has without tracing through inheritance chains. There are no 'where did this field come from?' moments. For team onboarding, this makes the codebase easier to navigate — you can grep for the type name and find all its attributes in one place. The trade-off is that there's some repetition: if two entity types share a concept (like 'id' or 'description'), each defines it independently rather than inheriting a shared definition. This is intentional — it keeps each entity self-contained and makes the data model easier to serialize to JSON without worrying about prototype chains or class metadata. When teaching new contributors, emphasize that adding a new entity type means adding one new interface and one new handler — no superclass changes needed.

text: What causal, temporal, or triggering relationships exist? Which entities cause changes in, or are triggered by, others?

choices.text: No causal links — entities change independently
Direct causation — entity A creates or changes entity B in a predictable chain
Event-driven — state changes propagate as events through the network
Feedback loops — entities can influence each other in circular patterns

answer:
Causal and temporal relationships:

Direct causation chains:
1. User answers Question → Answer is created → Artifact extraction runs → Artifact dictionary is updated. This is a synchronous chain — each step triggers the next immediately.

2. All Questions in a Round are answered → Round is marked complete → Next Round is enabled (if within same series). This is a sequential chain — rounds within a series execute in order.

3. All Rounds in a Series are answered → Series is marked complete → Dependent Series are enabled. This triggers the dependency resolution for downstream series.

4. User requests Export → Export generation reads Session state + Artifact dictionary → Compiled document is written to disk. This is a demand-driven chain — exports happen only when requested.

Event-driven propagation: The Engine emits events at each transition point: question:presented, answer:submitted, artifact:extracted, round:completed, series:completed, session:completed. These events could be used for logging, analytics, or external integrations (though currently they're only used internally).

No feedback loops: The causal chains are strictly forward-moving. Answers don't cause questions to change (the framework is immutable). Artifacts don't cause earlier answers to change (extraction is one-way). This simplicity prevents infinite loops and makes the system predictable.

variants.architect: SPACE's causal relationships form a strict forward-only dependency graph — this is the critical architectural constraint that makes the entire system tractable. The causal chain is: Framework loading → Session creation → Series execution (ordered by DEPENDS_ON) → Round completion → Question presentation → Answer recording → Artifact extraction → Artifact consumption by downstream Series. Each link in this chain is deterministic: given the same Framework and the same answers, you always get the same artifacts and the same specification output. The temporal ordering within a Series is fixed (Round 1 → Round 2 → Round 3 → ...) and enforced by `src/engine/question-router.ts` which advances sequentially. The triggering relationship between Series is the most interesting: Series N doesn't just 'run after' Series N-1 — it can only start when its consumed artifacts are present in the Session's artifact dictionary. This is an event-driven pattern where the 'event' is 'all required artifacts are available.' The absence of backward causation is deliberate: an artifact produced by Series 3 cannot be modified by Series 4. This constraint simplifies reasoning about the system (no cycles to worry about) and enables snapshot-based resumption (each snapshot captures the complete state at a point in time, and you can always resume from any snapshot because there are no dependencies pointing backward).
variants.practitioner: The causal chain is implemented as a pipeline in `src/engine/core.ts` where the main loop calls `processSeries(framework, session, seriesIndex)` sequentially for each Series in execution order. Within each Series, `completeRound()` processes questions in order, and after each answer is recorded, `extractArtifacts(answer, session)` is called synchronously. The temporal ordering is enforced by the `question-router.ts` which maintains a `currentRoundIndex` and `currentQuestionIndex` — advancing is the only valid operation (no going back to previous questions within a session, though re-answering by restarting is possible). The triggering mechanism for Series transitions is in `src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts`: `canStartSeries(series, session)` checks that `series.consumes.every(key => key in session.artifacts)`. This is a synchronous check, not an event listener — the system polls for readiness rather than reacting to events. For the artifact dictionary, which 'grows monotonically,' the implementation uses `session.artifacts = { ...session.artifacts, ...newArtifacts }` — a shallow merge. This means if two Series produce artifacts with the same key, the later one overwrites the earlier one. The framework JSON should ensure artifact keys are unique, but there's no runtime enforcement. A defensive pattern would be to use `Map<string, Artifact>` and throw on duplicate keys: `if (session.artifacts.has(key)) throw new Error('Duplicate artifact key')`. The snapshot system in `src/engine/snapshot-manager.ts` captures the artifact dictionary state after each Series completes, enabling resume-from-snapshot without re-running completed Series.
variants.strategist: The forward-only causal chain is the product's secret weapon: it makes SPACE's output deterministic and reproducible. Two users who provide the same answers to the same questions will get the same specification document. This is critical for adoption in teams — specifications must be reproducible for review and iteration. The triggering mechanism (Series starts only when dependencies are met) enables a natural 'work at your own pace' workflow: users can complete Series 1 and 2 in one session, then return days later to do Series 3, and the system will correctly resume with all artifacts from Series 1-2 intact. From a competitive perspective, this deterministic progression is what separates SPACE from AI chatbots — ChatGPT can generate a specification, but it's non-deterministic (different conversations produce different outputs). SPACE's 326 structured questions produce a consistent, comprehensive specification every time. The business value proposition is: 'SPACE gives you the same quality specification that a senior architect would produce in a week, in 2-3 hours of focused questioning.' The deterministic nature also enables a powerful marketing feature: 'compare' mode, where two completed sessions can be diffed to show what changed when requirements evolved. The risk is that the forward-only constraint limits flexibility — users sometimes want to go back and change early answers based on later insights. The mitigation is the 're-answer' feature (overwrite an answer and re-extract artifacts), but the UX for this needs careful design to avoid confusion about which artifacts are stale.
variants.ethicist: The causal chains in SPACE — user answers question → answer recorded → artifact extracted → session updated → auto-saved — create a deterministic pipeline where each step is an irreversible commitment. Once an answer is submitted and artifacts are extracted, the system moves forward. This design raises ethical questions about informed consent and reversibility. Users may not fully understand that submitting an answer triggers a cascade of automated processing including LLM-powered auto-fill (which introduces external AI judgment into their specification) and artifact generation (which infers implications beyond what they explicitly stated). The temporal coupling between answer submission and artifact extraction means that users cannot preview the full consequences of their answer before committing it. The auto-save timer introduces another temporal concern: even if a user is mid-thought, the system periodically snapshots their incomplete state, potentially preserving half-formed ideas as if they were final decisions. For collaborative teams where session files are shared, this creates a transparency problem — exported specifications may contain artifacts inferred by the system from partial answers, but the recipient has no way to distinguish between what the user explicitly stated and what the system automatically generated. The causal chain from Framework → Engine → Session → Export also means that the structural assumptions of the Framework propagate through every output, making the final specification's worldview a product of the framework designer's choices, not just the user's.
variants.futurist: SPACE's synchronous causal chain (answer → artifact → advance) will be replaced by asynchronous, event-driven pipelines within 3-5 years. The current model processes each answer immediately and linearly — this works for a single-user CLI tool but won't survive the transition to AI-assisted collaborative specification. Future tools will decouple answer capture from artifact generation: users will answer questions at their own pace, and background AI workers will continuously re-generate artifacts as new answers arrive, potentially producing draft specifications before the user has finished the question sequence. The trigger model will shift from explicit 'submit answer' to implicit inference: AI agents will observe the user's conversation with the tool and auto-capture specification decisions without requiring formal question-by-question interaction. The auto-save timer is a primitive form of event sourcing — within a decade, the full interaction history (keystrokes, hesitations, revisions, skips) will be the primary data model, and the answer/answer pairs will be projections derived from that richer event stream. The causal chain from Framework to Export will also reverse: instead of Framework structure causing export format, the desired export format will cause the Framework to dynamically restructure itself, asking different questions based on what the target document requires.
variants.educator: The causal chain in SPACE is the 'what happens when I press Enter' flow. Understanding this chain is crucial for debugging and for knowing what to expect: when you submit an answer, four things happen in sequence. First, the answer is recorded in your Session. Second, the artifact extraction engine processes your answer and updates the Artifact dictionary — this is where the system 'understands' your answer and generates structured data from it. Third, the engine advances to the next question. Fourth, the auto-save timer eventually writes everything to disk. If you ever wonder 'why didn't my answer show up in the export,' trace this chain: was the answer recorded? Did artifact extraction succeed? The answer text in src/engine/core.ts (the submitAnswer function) is the single place to understand this flow. For learners, the key insight is that artifact extraction is automatic and happens on every answer — you don't need to trigger it. But it also means that poorly worded answers may produce unexpected artifacts. A common beginner pattern is to give vague answers and then be surprised by the specificity of the generated artifacts. Teaching tip: show new users the artifact extraction output after their first few answers so they understand the causal relationship between answer clarity and artifact quality.

text: What dependency chains, prerequisites, or ordering constraints exist? Must some entities exist before others can be created or used?

choices.text: No ordering constraints — entities are independent
Simple chain — a linear sequence of prerequisites
Branching dependencies — a DAG of ordered entity relationships
Cyclic dependencies — entities depend on each other (requires careful management)

answer:
Dependency chains and ordering constraints:

Series dependency graph (DAG):
- Series 1: no dependencies (can start immediately)
- Series 2: depends on [1] (must wait for Series 1)
- Series 3: depends on [2] (must wait for Series 2)
- Series 4: depends on [2, 3] (must wait for both)
- Series 5: depends on [1, 4] (must wait for both)
- Series 6: depends on [4, 5] (must wait for both)
- Series 7: depends on [5, 6] (must wait for both)

This creates a diamond-shaped DAG with Series 1 at the root and Series 7 at the leaf. The critical path is 1→2→3→4→5→6→7 (7 steps).

Within each series, rounds execute sequentially (Round 1 before Round 2, etc.). Within each round, questions can execute in any order (no inter-question dependencies within a round).

The dependency resolution algorithm: When the Engine needs the next question, it (1) identifies the first incomplete series whose dependencies are all met, (2) finds the first incomplete round in that series, (3) selects the first unanswered question in that round. If no series has all dependencies met (e.g., all remaining series are blocked), the session is complete.

Practical implication: A user who answers all of Series 1 can immediately jump to Series 2 (once Series 1 completes). They cannot skip to Series 3 without completing Series 2. This enforced ordering ensures that each series has the context it needs from predecessor series.

variants.architect: SPACE's dependency structure is a **directed acyclic graph (DAG) with a critical path** — the longest chain of sequential dependencies determines the minimum time to complete a full specification. The critical path is: Framework load → Series 1 (3 Rounds, ~15 Questions) → Series 2 (depends on Series 1) → Series 3 (depends on Series 2) → Series 4 (depends on Series 1, 3) → Series 5 (depends on Series 1, 4) → Series 6 (depends on Series 4, 5) → Series 7 (depends on Series 5, 6). This is essentially a linear chain with some parallelism possible between Series that don't depend on each other. Within each Series, the ordering constraint is: Round N must complete before Round N+1 starts (enforced by question-router), and within a Round, Questions can theoretically be presented in any order but are presented sequentially for UX simplicity. The prerequisite structure creates a 'information funnel' pattern: early Series (1-2) gather broad, foundational information; middle Series (3-4) refine and structure it; late Series (5-7) add implementation details. Each Series' prerequisites are not just ordering constraints but semantic prerequisites — Series 3 (relationships) can't produce meaningful artifacts without Series 2 (entities) because relationships reference entities. This semantic coupling is stronger than the formal DEPENDS_ON constraint.
variants.practitioner: The dependency ordering is implemented in `src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts` with a topological sort algorithm. The `buildExecutionOrder(framework)` function constructs a graph from the `series.deps` arrays and returns a valid execution order. For SPACE's 7-Series framework, the order is typically [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] (linear), but the framework JSON could define a different dependency graph (e.g., if Series 3 and 4 were independent of each other but both depended on Series 2, they could run in parallel — though the CLI is sequential so this parallelism isn't exploited). The prerequisite validation happens at two points: (1) before starting a Series (`canStartSeries()` checks `series.deps.every(dep => isSeriesComplete(dep))`) and (2) before accessing an artifact (`session.getArtifact(key)` throws if the key doesn't exist). The ordering within a Series is enforced by `question-router.ts` which tracks `currentRoundIndex` and only advances to the next round after `completeRound()` returns. For the '67 Questions across 7 Series' structure, the prerequisite chain means the user must complete all Questions in Series 1 before seeing any Question in Series 2. The implementation uses `framework.series[i].rounds` to navigate the structure. A practical edge case: if a user starts a session, completes Series 1-3, then updates the framework.json to add new Questions to Series 1, the session should still be resumable because the session stores completed Questions by ID, and new Questions simply appear as unanswered. The dependency resolver doesn't need to re-validate completed Series — it only checks Series that haven't started yet.
variants.strategist: The dependency chain structure is directly responsible for SPACE's user experience arc: it creates a natural 'journey' from abstract vision (Series 1) to concrete implementation (Series 7). This progression mirrors how experienced developers think about projects — start with the big picture, then refine — and that's exactly what the target audience expects. The prerequisite structure also enables a powerful onboarding feature: 'quick start mode' where users can answer only Series 1 and get a high-level specification, then come back later for the detailed Series 2-7. This is important for adoption because the full 326-question journey takes 2-3 hours, which is a significant time commitment. The dependency graph also creates natural pause points between Series — each Series completion is a milestone that produces tangible output (artifacts), which gives users a sense of progress. For the product roadmap, the dependency structure should support future features like: (1) parallel Series execution for web-based collaboration (two team members work on different Series simultaneously), (2) conditional Series (skip Series 7 if the project doesn't need deployment), and (3) iterative refinement (re-run a single Series with new answers without re-running all upstream Series). The risk of the current linear dependency chain is that it forces users through the entire journey even if they only need a specific part of the specification. A future version could allow 'Series selection' where users pick which Series to run, with the dependency resolver automatically including prerequisite Series.
variants.ethicist: The mandatory dependency chain in SPACE — Series 1 before Series 2, Series 2 before Series 3, and so on — enforces a linear progression that assumes one 'correct' order for thinking about a system. This is epistemologically loaded. Real-world system design doesn't follow a strict linear progression: architects often revisit conceptual decisions after learning about infrastructure constraints, or refine data models after understanding performance requirements. By locking Series 2 (Structural Depth) behind Series 1 (Conceptual Depth), the tool assumes that conceptual understanding must precede structural analysis — a valid but not universal pedagogical choice. This ordering has consequences: users who think structurally first (bottom-up thinkers, for instance) are forced into a top-down progression that may not match their natural cognitive process. The prerequisite model also creates an accessibility barrier: users who are partially filling in a specification for an existing system (rather than designing from scratch) may have structural answers ready but be forced to generate conceptual answers first. The dependency model could be seen as a form of intellectual paternalism — the framework decides the order of thinking, and the user must comply. For organizations using SPACE as a standard process tool, this locks in one methodology for requirements gathering, potentially marginalizing teams that use different frameworks (domain-driven design, behavior-driven development, etc.) that define their own ordering.
variants.futurist: The rigid sequential dependency between Series will be the first architectural constraint to break as SPACE evolves toward AI-native operation. Within three years, expect a dependency graph that's advisory rather than mandatory: the system will recommend completing Series 1 before Series 2 but will allow skipping ahead, with AI filling in conceptual gaps from structural answers provided later. This reflects a broader trend in developer tools: moving from prescriptive workflows to adaptive ones. The concept of 'prerequisites' in question-ordering will transform into 'context weight' — the system will dynamically adjust how much context from prior Series influences current questions, rather than enforcing binary blocking. In a world where LLMs can infer conceptual frameworks from structural descriptions, the strict dependency chain becomes an artificial constraint that slows power users without helping novices. Future versions will likely implement a confidence-weighted dependency model: if the AI can infer that a user's answers to Series 3 questions are consistent with a hypothetical Series 1 completion, it will allow progression while flagging the conceptual gaps. The dependency graph will also become bidirectional — answering a Series 4 question might trigger a 'revisit' recommendation for a Series 2 question where the new information creates inconsistency.
variants.educator: Understanding why Series must be completed in order is key to using SPACE effectively. The dependency chain exists because each Series builds context that later Series need. Series 1 (Conceptual Depth) establishes what the system is and why it exists. Series 2 (Structural Depth) builds on that to define the components. Series 3 adds behavioral details, Series 4 addresses data, and so on. Think of it like building a house: you need the foundation (Series 1) before the frame (Series 2) before the walls (Series 3). You can't wire electrical (Series 5) before you know where the walls are. For new users, the dependency chain is actually helpful — it prevents the common problem of specification paralysis where you don't know where to start. SPACE gives you a guided path. The dependency also serves a documentation purpose: when someone reads your exported specification, the questions are in logical order, making the document easier to follow. Team leads should communicate this ordering to their teams so everyone understands why they can't jump to the infrastructure questions (Series 5) without first answering the conceptual questions (Series 1). If a team member has strong opinions about infrastructure but hasn't answered the conceptual questions yet, encourage them to use the artifact system to capture those ideas as notes — they'll be able to reference them when they reach Series 5.

text: What rules govern how relationships can change? Can associations be created, deleted, or modified at any time, or are there restrictions?

choices.text: Freely mutable — relationships can change at any time with no restrictions
State-gated — relationships can only change when entities are in certain states
Immutable after creation — relationships are set once and cannot change
Versioned — relationship changes create new versions rather than modifying in place

answer:
Rules governing relationship changes:

Framework relationships (Series→Round→Question→Choice): Immutable. These are defined in JSON files and never change at runtime. The framework is a read-only reference.

Session relationships: Mutable with constraints.
- Session→Answer: Answers can be added (new questions answered) or updated (re-answering a question). Cannot be deleted (skipping is recorded as a "skipped" answer, not deletion).
- Session→Artifact: Artifacts can be added (new extraction) or updated (refined extraction). Cannot be deleted (artifacts are append-only with overwrite semantics).
- Session→Project: Immutable after creation. A session belongs to one project forever.

Export relationships: Regenerated, not modified. When an export is stale (new answers since last export), it's regenerated from scratch, not incrementally updated. The old export is overwritten.

Answer→Question: Immutable. Once an answer is linked to a question, the link doesn't change. If the framework changes (which it doesn't), orphaned answers would reference non-existent questions — this is handled by the "missing question" edge case (answer preserved but marked as orphaned).

The immutability of framework relationships is a key design decision: it ensures deterministic behavior. The Engine always sees the same framework structure, regardless of when it was loaded or how many sessions have been created. This eliminates an entire class of bugs related to framework evolution.

variants.architect: SPACE enforces a **append-only mutation model** for the Framework hierarchy and a **replace-only mutation model** for the Session hierarchy. Framework entities (Series, Rounds, Questions, Choices) are immutable at runtime — once loaded from JSON, they cannot be created, deleted, or modified. This is enforced by loading the framework into a readonly structure in `src/data/framework-loader.ts` and passing it as `Readonly<Framework>` to the Engine. Session entities (Answers, Artifacts) support replacement but not deletion — you can overwrite an Answer by re-answering a question, and artifacts are replaced when re-extracted, but there's no 'delete answer' operation. This simplifies the state management significantly: there's no undo stack, no soft-delete, no version history. The rule for Framework evolution is external: new versions of framework.json can be released with new Series, new Questions, or modified Choices, but existing sessions reference questions by ID, so they remain valid. The creation/deletion lifecycle is: Framework entities are created during framework loading and destroyed when the process exits (no persistence needed because they're loaded from the immutable JSON source). Session entities are created during the session and persisted to disk after each operation (in `src/storage/filesystem.ts`). Export entities are created during export and persisted as files (they're the final output of the pipeline).
variants.practitioner: The mutation rules are implemented through TypeScript's type system and runtime validation. Framework loading in `src/data/framework-loader.ts` returns `Framework` objects that are never modified — the Engine receives them as function parameters (pass by value in terms of structure) rather than storing references to mutable objects. In `src/engine/session-manager.ts`, `session.answers.set(questionId, answer)` replaces an existing answer if the questionId already exists — this is the 'replace-only' semantics. The artifact dictionary is updated via `session.artifacts = { ...session.artifacts, ...newArtifacts }`, which also replaces on key collision. There's no explicit deletion: if you want to 'remove' an answer, you set it to an empty answer object `{ questionId, text: '', followUpChoiceId: null }`. For Framework versioning, `src/data/framework-loader.ts` validates the framework JSON against a schema at load time — if a new version has structural changes (different number of Series, new required fields), the validator will catch it and either adapt gracefully or abort with an error. The Export entities in `src/export/index.ts` are write-once: once a file is written to disk, it's not modified. If you re-export, the old file is overwritten entirely. The filesystem storage in `src/storage/filesystem.ts` uses `fs.writeFileSync()` which atomically replaces the file contents — no partial writes, no corruption risk from interrupted writes.
variants.strategist: The append-only/replace-only mutation model is a deliberate simplification that aligns with SPACE's positioning as a specification tool, not an editor. Users don't need to 'delete' answers — they re-answer, which is faster and more natural. The absence of version history is a strategic trade-off: it keeps the tool simple and the file format small, but it means users can't track how their specification evolved over time. This is acceptable for v1 because the primary use case is 'write a specification once,' not 'iterate on a specification over weeks.' However, for the product roadmap, version history should be a priority feature: it enables 'specification diffing' (compare two versions of a specification to see what changed), 'rollback' (revert to a previous version if the current one is wrong), and 'collaboration' (see who changed what). The external Framework evolution model is strategically important: it means SPACE can release new Framework versions with better questions without breaking existing sessions. This is the same pattern used by database migration tools (Flyway, Alembic) — the schema evolves, but existing data remains valid. The risk is Framework version fragmentation: if different users are on different Framework versions, their specifications aren't directly comparable. The mitigation is to include the Framework version in every Session file and in every Export, so users know which Framework produced a given specification.
variants.ethicist: The immutability of Framework relationships versus the mutability of Project relationships creates a two-tier system of trust and control. The Framework — where questions live, how they're ordered, what choices are offered — is permanently frozen once loaded. Users cannot add questions, reorder Series, or modify choices to better fit their context. This means the system's assessment of what matters is unchangeable by the people using it. From an equity perspective, this is significant: the Framework was designed by specific people with specific assumptions about software specification, and those assumptions are now structurally locked. Users from underrepresented domains — embedded systems, accessibility-first design, sustainable computing — cannot modify the Framework to reflect their priorities. Meanwhile, the Project relationships (Session → Answer, Session → Artifact) are fully mutable: users can change answers, and artifacts re-extract. This mutability gives users control over their outputs but not over the questions that shape those outputs. The snapshot and undo mechanisms provide some recourse, but they operate within the constraints of the Framework. An ethical improvement would be allowing community-contributed Framework variants — different question sets designed for different domains, cultural contexts, or regulatory environments — while maintaining the immutability guarantee within a single Framework instance.
variants.futurist: The immutability of Framework relationships is a design choice that will become untenable as specification tools evolve. Within five years, the Framework will be a living, adaptable structure — not a static JSON file. Expect Framework-as-code: question structures defined in TypeScript or Python that can be version-controlled, branched, merged, and community-contributed. The immutability guarantee will shift from 'cannot change' to 'changes are tracked and reversible' — like Git for your question structure. This enables domain-specific Framework forks: healthcare, fintech, climate tech, and gaming would each maintain specialized question trees that diverge from the core Framework while sharing common foundations. The mutability of Project relationships will also evolve: instead of the current 'change answer → re-extract artifacts' pattern, expect undo trees with branching — users can explore multiple answer paths for the same question and compare the resulting artifact divergences. The snapshot mechanism will transform from a manual save into continuous event logging, enabling arbitrary point-in-time queries ('what did my specification look like before I changed the architecture decision?'). The contrast between immutable Framework and mutable Project will dissolve as both become version-controlled, diffable, and mergeable.
variants.educator: The rule to remember is: you can change your answers, but you can't change the questions. Framework relationships (how questions are organized into Rounds, Rounds into Series) are read-only — the system loads them from JSON files and never modifies them. Project relationships (your answers, artifacts, and exports) are fully writable. This matters practically because if you realize your answer to question 3.2.1 was wrong, you can go back and change it — the artifact extraction will re-run and update accordingly. But you cannot add a question about 'accessibility requirements' to Series 1 if the Framework doesn't include one. For teams using SPACE, this means: if you need custom questions, you'll need to modify the Framework JSON files directly (see the Framework authoring guide in the documentation). Once you've modified them, those modifications persist across sessions because the Framework files live in your project directory. The practical implication for learners: don't worry about making mistakes in your answers — they're fully reversible. Focus your energy on understanding the questions being asked, because those are the fixed constraints you're working within.

text: How do relationships compose or chain across entities? Can indirect relationships be inferred from direct ones?

choices.text: No composition — only direct relationships matter
Transitive — some relationship types imply transitive chains
Composable — relationships can be combined according to specific rules
Weighted/typed composition — chains have strength or type that affects meaning

answer:
Relationship composition and chaining:

Direct relationships: Framework→Series, Series→Round, Round→Question, Question→Choice. These are the only relationships defined in the framework JSON.

Indirect relationships (derived from direct):
- Framework→Question: derived through Series and Round. The path is Framework→Series→Round→Question. This path is used for question numbering (the full ID encodes the path: "2.3.1" means Series 2, Round 3, Question 1).
- Framework→Choice: derived through Series, Round, and Question. Used for answer validation (a choice must belong to the correct question).
- Session→Question: derived through the current_question_id pointer. The session tracks which question it's currently on, creating an implicit relationship.

Transitive chains: The dependency graph creates transitive chains. If Series 4 depends on Series 2 and 3, and Series 3 depends on Series 2, then Series 4 transitively depends on Series 2 through two paths (direct and through Series 3). The dependency resolution algorithm handles this correctly — it checks direct dependencies, not transitive ones, because the transitive dependencies are already satisfied by the direct ones.

Composable relationships: The artifact consumption pattern composes relationships across series. Series 3 consumes entity_list (produced by Series 2), and Series 4 consumes entity_list + relationship_graph (produced by Series 2 + 3). The composition is additive — later series consume artifacts from all predecessor series.

Weighted composition: Not applicable in the current system. All relationships are binary (exists/doesn't exist) with no weights or strengths. This is appropriate for a specification tool — there's no concept of "weakly related" or "strongly associated" in the question framework.

variants.architect: The indirect relationships in SPACE are traversable via **ID-based resolution chains** — the most powerful pattern in the system. Starting from any entity, you can reach any other entity by following a chain of ID references: Export → Session (by sessionId) → Answer (by questionId) → Question (by questionId) → Round (by containment) → Series (by containment) → Framework (by containment). This chain is unidirectional (parent → child via containment, child → parent via ID reference) and has a maximum length of 6 hops. The indirect relationship composition is most valuable for **provenance tracking**: given an Export, you can trace back through every artifact, every answer, every question, to produce a complete audit trail of how the specification was generated. The chain: Export → Session → Artifacts → (consumed by) Series → (produced by) Answers → Questions → Rounds → Series → Framework. This is implemented in the export formatters (`src/export/formatters/`) where each exporter can optionally include provenance metadata. The indirect relationship resolution is lazy — the system doesn't pre-compute the full relationship graph. When you need to find 'all Exports that reference a specific Answer's Question,' you scan all Exports, resolve their Session, and check the Session's Answers. This is O(n) where n is the number of Exports, which is fine because n is small (typically 1-5). The cross-boundary traversal (Framework → Session) is the most interesting: a Question in the Framework can be linked to an Answer in the Session via `session.answers.get(question.id)`. This traversal happens thousands of times during a session (once per question in the progress tracker) and must be fast — the Map-based storage in Session ensures O(1) lookups.
variants.practitioner: The indirect relationship traversal is implemented as a series of accessor methods across the codebase. In `src/engine/question-router.ts`, navigating from a Question back to its parent Round and Series is done via the Framework tree: `framework.series[s].rounds[r].questions[q]` — the indices are computed from the question's position in the flat question list. In `src/export/formatters/markdown-exporter.ts`, provenance tracking works by following the chain: export the Artifact → include `artifact.sourceQuestionId` → look up the Question text → include the Question text as a 'Source:' annotation in the Markdown output. The key implementation for cross-boundary traversal is in `src/engine/progress.ts`: `isQuestionAnswered(question, session)` checks `session.answers.has(question.id)` — this is the primary cross-boundary check, happening for all 326 questions during progress computation. The implementation uses a breadth-first traversal of the Framework tree, checking each Question against the Session's answer Map. For relationship graph traversal (Series → consumed artifacts → producing Series), the implementation in `src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts` builds a static graph at session start: `buildDependencyGraph(framework)` returns `Map<string, string[]>` mapping Series IDs to their dependency Series IDs. This graph is computed once and reused for all dependency checks. A performance concern: the relationship graph is rebuilt from scratch when resuming a session, even if the framework hasn't changed. Caching the graph in the Session object would avoid this recomputation. For the 'traversable from any entity' claim, the practical limitation is that Choice entities are not directly linked back to their parent Question in the data model — the Question → Choice relationship is parent-to-child containment, but Choice doesn't have a `parentQuestionId` field. To traverse from Choice back to Question, you need to search the Framework tree.
variants.strategist: The indirect relationship composition is what makes SPACE's output more valuable than a simple questionnaire's output. The provenance chain (Export → Session → Answer → Question → Round → Series → Framework) enables a feature that no competitor offers: **specification traceability**. Every line in the generated specification can be traced back to the exact question that produced it, the answer that was given, and the artifact that was extracted. This is invaluable for specification review — a reviewer can look at a specific claim in the specification and verify its source. This traceability is a key differentiator for enterprise adoption: compliance teams can audit how specifications were generated, which is important for regulated industries (healthcare, finance, government). The indirect relationship traversal also enables the 'specification comparison' feature: two Exports from different Sessions can be compared by following the provenance chain to identify which answers changed and how those changes propagated through the artifact graph. This is the 'git diff for specifications' concept that would be a major marketing feature. The lazy resolution approach (no pre-computed relationship graph) is fine for CLI usage but would be a bottleneck for a web-based dashboard that needs to display the full relationship graph. A web version should pre-compute and cache the relationship graph in a database, enabling O(1) lookups for any relationship query.
variants.ethicist: SPACE's ability to infer indirect relationships — deriving Round-level knowledge from Question answers, or Series-level insights from accumulated Artifacts — creates a transparency concern. Users provide answers at the Question level, but the system synthesizes higher-level conclusions they never explicitly endorsed. When a user answers five individual questions about authentication, the system infers a 'security posture' Artifact that may attribute intent or sophistication the user never claimed. This inferential composition is valuable for specification completeness but ethically fraught: it attributes beliefs, strategies, or architectural decisions to the user based on patterns across answers. In regulated industries, this is particularly problematic — a specification document that includes system-level inferences derived from individual answers could be treated as a formal statement of intent, liability, or compliance. The relationship chaining also means that a single poorly-worded answer can cascade into multiple downstream Artifacts, compounding error. There's no explicit 'I didn't mean that' mechanism — once artifacts are extracted, the user must manually inspect and override each one. For collaborative teams, the risk is that team members trust the composed output as authoritative without verifying that each individual answer supports the inferred conclusions.
variants.futurist: The current indirect relationship inference — where artifact extraction synthesizes cross-question patterns — is a primitive form of what will become full semantic graph traversal. Within three years, the relationship chain will expand from 'Answer → Artifact' to 'Answer → Embedding → Knowledge Graph Node → Related Nodes → Cross-Domain Artifacts.' The system will maintain a vector representation of every answer and find relationships that span Series boundaries in ways that the current linear artifact extraction cannot. For instance, an answer about data volume in Series 4 might automatically generate a performance concern Artifact in Series 5 without being explicitly routed through the artifact extraction pipeline. The composition model will become recursive: Artifacts generated from Answers will themselves be treated as inputs to higher-order inference, creating layered synthesis that mirrors how human architects reason about systems. Within a decade, the 'indirect relationship' concept will be the primary output mode — users will answer direct questions, and the system will generate a complete specification through multi-hop reasoning across the entire knowledge graph. The explicit 'question → answer → artifact' pipeline will become a fallback for simple cases, with the AI reasoning engine handling complex cross-domain inference as the default.
variants.educator: Relationship composition in SPACE means that your individual answers add up to bigger insights. When you answer a question about database choices, the system doesn't just store that one answer — it uses your answer, combined with your other answers about scale, data types, and access patterns, to generate higher-level artifacts like 'storage architecture' or 'data strategy.' This is like writing individual paragraphs for an essay: each paragraph is a standalone answer, but the essay's argument emerges from how they relate to each other. Understanding this helps you give better answers. If you know that your answer about database technology will be combined with your answer about expected user count, write both answers with that combination in mind. For team onboarding, demonstrate this by showing the Artifact dictionary after answering 10 questions — point out how the system has started connecting dots between individual answers. The key learning: individual answer quality matters less than answer consistency across related questions. A technically correct answer that contradicts your other answers will produce confusing Artifacts. Teach teams to think about each answer in the context of their other answers, not in isolation.

text: What is the overall scope of the procedure or workflow? What does it start from and what is its end state?

choices.text: Narrow — a single well-defined task with clear boundaries
Moderate — an end-to-end process with several stages
Broad — a multi-phase workflow spanning distinct sub-processes

answer:
Overall procedure scope: End-to-end specification generation spanning 7 phases (one per series).

Start state: User has a project idea or system to specify. No prior documentation, no existing specification, no code. Just a concept in their head.

End state: A comprehensive, multi-format specification document that captures domain context, entities, relationships, procedures, technical requirements, methodology, and operational preferences. The specification is machine-readable (JSON/YAML), human-readable (Markdown/HTML), and LLM-consumable (prompt format).

The procedure is moderate in scope — it's not a single atomic task (too narrow) and not a multi-phase program (too broad). It's an interactive elicitation session that takes 1-4 hours depending on depth of answers and number of questions answered.

Sub-processes: (1) Project initialization — create project directory, load framework, configure LLM provider. (2) Interactive question flow — present questions, collect answers, extract artifacts. (3) Artifact accumulation — build the artifact dictionary across all series. (4) Export compilation — generate specification documents in requested formats. (5) Session management — save, resume, abandon sessions.

The procedure is interactive (requires human input at each step) but structured (the framework determines the question order). The human provides domain knowledge; the system provides structure and extraction.

variants.architect: SPACE's procedure scope is a **complete specification lifecycle** — from blank project to multi-format specification output. The procedure starts with project initialization (creating a project directory, loading the Framework, instantiating a Session) and ends with specification export (compiling all artifacts into multiple output formats). This is a well-bounded scope because it has clear entry conditions (framework JSON exists, user provides project name) and clear exit conditions (all 7 Series completed, all exports written to disk). The procedure is not a single monolithic flow but rather a **nested procedure pattern**: the top-level procedure manages the session lifecycle, and each Series contains its own sub-procedure (present questions, collect answers, extract artifacts). The scope boundary is important: SPACE does NOT include project management (creating tickets, assigning tasks), implementation (writing code), or deployment (pushing to production). These are explicitly out of scope — the procedure ends when the specification is written. The procedure also supports interruption and resumption: at any point, the user can Ctrl+C, and the session state is saved. The procedure resumes from the exact point of interruption. This is critical for a 2-3 hour procedure — no user will complete it in one sitting. The scope is defined by the 326 Questions across 7 Series, with each Question requiring both an open-ended text answer and a follow-up choice selection.
variants.practitioner: The procedure lifecycle is implemented in `src/engine/core.ts` as the main entry point. The `runSession(frameworkPath, projectName)` function orchestrates the entire procedure: (1) `loadFramework(frameworkPath)` in `src/data/framework-loader.ts` parses the JSON and validates the structure, (2) `createSession(projectName)` in `src/engine/session-manager.ts` initializes the Session object and persists it, (3) the main loop iterates over Series in dependency order: `for (const seriesId of executionOrder) { await processSeries(framework, session, seriesId) }`, (4) `exportSession(session, formats)` in `src/export/index.ts` writes the output files. The entry point is `src/cli/commands/run.ts` which parses CLI arguments and calls `runSession()`. The scope boundaries are enforced by the Engine — there's no 'create ticket' or 'write code' functionality because those methods don't exist. The interruption handling uses Node.js signal handlers: `process.on('SIGINT', () => { saveSession(session); process.exit(0) })` in `src/engine/core.ts`. The session file is written atomically (write to temp file, then rename) in `src/storage/filesystem.ts` to prevent corruption from mid-write interruptions. The resume logic checks for an existing session file: `if (sessionFileExists(projectName)) { loadSession(projectName) } else { createSession(projectName) }`. The 326-Question scope is defined by the framework JSON, not hardcoded in the Engine — the Engine processes whatever Framework it's given.
variants.strategist: The procedure scope of 'blank project to specification output' is the right boundary for an MVP. It's comprehensive enough to produce real value (a complete specification document) while being narrow enough to ship quickly (no project management, no code generation, no deployment). The 2-3 hour completion time is a double-edged sword: it's long enough to produce a thorough specification (which is the value) but long enough to cause abandonment (which is the risk). The mitigation is the resume feature, which is essential. From a product strategy perspective, the procedure scope should be extended in phases: v1 covers the core lifecycle (current scope), v2 adds 'quick start' mode (answer Series 1 only for a high-level spec), v3 adds 'update mode' (re-run a single Series with new answers), v4 adds 'collaborative mode' (multiple users contribute to the same specification). Each phase extends the scope incrementally without changing the core procedure. The key metric for the current scope is completion rate: what percentage of users who start a session complete all 7 Series? If it's below 30%, the scope needs to be reduced (fewer Questions, shorter procedure). If it's above 50%, the scope is right. The competitive advantage of the current scope is that it produces a complete, structured specification — most competitor tools (ChatGPT, Notion AI) produce partial, unstructured output that requires significant manual cleanup.
variants.ethicist: SPACE's end-to-end scope — from empty project to exported specification — implicitly defines what a 'complete' system specification looks like. This definition carries ethical weight because it determines what aspects of a system are considered important enough to ask about, and what aspects are excluded entirely. The 7-Series framework covers concepts, structure, behavior, data, infrastructure, software, and performance — but not security (except as covered by individual questions), not accessibility, not environmental impact, not community impact, not labor implications. By defining the scope of specification, SPACE defines the scope of consideration. Systems specified through SPACE are more likely to address the 7 covered areas and less likely to address the uncovered ones, because the tool's structure makes covered areas salient and uncovered areas invisible. For organizations mandating SPACE as their specification tool, this creates a systematic blind spot: entire categories of ethical consideration (privacy-by-design, environmental sustainability, accessibility compliance, algorithmic fairness) may be systematically omitted because the Framework doesn't ask about them. The scope definition is also culturally situated: the 7-Series structure reflects Western engineering traditions that separate 'what' from 'how' from 'where' — other traditions might integrate these concerns from the start.
variants.futurist: SPACE's current scope — a linear journey from conceptualization through infrastructure — will expand dramatically as the tool evolves. Within five years, the procedure will likely extend to include: security threat modeling as a parallel thread running through all Series, accessibility compliance checks at each decision point, environmental impact assessment (carbon footprint of infrastructure choices), and regulatory compliance mapping. The 7-Series structure will become insufficient as AI-native specification tools enable dynamic scope adjustment — the system will expand or contract the procedure based on the domain. A climate-tech project might get an expanded Series on environmental impact, while a fintech project gets expanded compliance and audit Series. The scope will also evolve from 'specification generation' to 'specification lifecycle management' — the procedure won't end at export but continue through deployment, monitoring, and evolution. Within a decade, SPACE-type tools will maintain living specifications that update themselves as the system's actual behavior diverges from the specification, creating a continuous feedback loop between the procedure and reality. The start state will also change: instead of starting from 'a project idea,' future versions will start from 'an existing codebase' and extract specifications through code analysis.
variants.educator: The scope of SPACE's procedure covers the full journey from 'I have an idea' to 'I have a complete specification document.' Understanding this scope helps set expectations for new users. The procedure starts when you create a project (CLI: space init <name>) and ends when you export your specification (CLI: space export). Between those two points, you'll answer questions across 7 Series, each building on the last. For team leads onboarding their teams, communicate the time commitment upfront: a full specification typically takes 2-4 hours for an experienced developer, longer for complex systems. The scope also helps with partial usage — teams don't have to complete the entire procedure. You can run SPACE for just Series 1 (Conceptual Depth) to generate a high-level concept document, then use that as input to your existing specification process. Or you can use only the export functionality to format previously answered questions into a document. For educators building training materials, the scope map is your curriculum outline: each Series is a module, each Round is a lesson, each Question is an exercise. The end-to-end journey from empty project to exported spec is the capstone project.

text: How many distinct steps, stages, or phases should the procedure contain? What is the natural breakdown?

choices.text: 2–4 steps — quick process with few handoffs
5–8 steps — moderate complexity with clear waypoints
9+ steps — comprehensive procedure with fine-grained stages

answer:
Step breakdown: 5-8 distinct stages with clear waypoints.

Stage 1: Initialize — Create project, load framework, verify environment. (CLI: "space init <name>")
Stage 2: Series 1 (Conceptual Depth) — 6 questions across 3 rounds. Establishes domain, audience, vocabulary. (~15 min)
Stage 3: Series 2 (Ontological Characteristics) — 15 questions across 5 rounds. Discovers entities, attributes, boundaries. (~30 min)
Stage 4: Series 3 (Semantic Relationships) — 8 questions across 4 rounds. Maps associations, hierarchies, causation. (~20 min)
Stage 5: Series 4 (Procedural Breadth) — 6 questions across 3 rounds. Defines workflows, decisions, error handling. (~15 min)
Stage 6: Series 5 (Technical Specifications) — 20 questions across 4 rounds. Captures hardware, software, performance, security. (~40 min)
Stage 7: Series 6 (Development Methodologies) — 6 questions across 3 rounds. Determines process, quality, communication. (~15 min)
Stage 8: Series 7 (Operational/Functional) — 6 questions across 3 rounds. Covers deployment, monitoring, maintenance. (~15 min)

Total: 67 questions. Average 2-3 minutes per question (reading, thinking, typing). Estimated session time: 2-3 hours for thorough answers, 30-45 minutes for quick answers.

Waypoints: Each series completion is a natural checkpoint. The session auto-saves after each answer, so any interruption preserves progress. The "space export" command can be run at any waypoint to generate a partial specification.

variants.architect: SPACE's procedure has **8 distinct stages** with a natural progression from definition (stages 1-2) through analysis (stages 3-4) to specification (stages 5-8). This is a 3-phase decomposition: Definition Phase (load framework, create session — trivial, <1 second), Interaction Phase (Series 1-7, each containing 3-5 Rounds of 2-5 Questions — this is the bulk of the procedure, 2-3 hours), and Export Phase (compile artifacts into output formats — fast, <10 seconds). The 8 stages map to the 7 Series plus initialization, which is the correct granularity — each stage produces distinct, independently valuable artifacts. The stage decomposition is justified by the information architecture: Series 1 (Vision) produces foundational artifacts that all subsequent Series consume. Series 2-3 (Entities, Relationships) produce the data model. Series 4 (Procedures) produces the behavioral model. Series 5-7 (Infrastructure, Team, Deployment) produce the implementation model. This mirrors the standard software architecture documentation flow: Vision → Data Model → Behavioral Model → Implementation. The stage count of 8 (including init) is appropriate because it creates natural pause points — each Series completion is a milestone that can be independently validated and reviewed. More stages (e.g., splitting Series into individual Rounds) would create too many checkpoints and slow the flow. Fewer stages (e.g., merging Series 2-3 into one) would create stages that are too large and hard to validate incrementally.
variants.practitioner: The 8 stages are implemented as a loop in `src/engine/core.ts`: Stage 1 is the Framework load (`loadFramework()`), Stage 2 is Session creation (`createSession()`), and Stages 3-8 correspond to `processSeries()` calls for Series 1-7. Each stage internally processes Rounds via `completeRound()`, which iterates over Questions via `askQuestion()`. The stage count is not hardcoded — it's determined by the Framework's Series count. The implementation in `src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts` computes the execution order dynamically, so if a custom Framework defines 5 Series or 10 Series, the procedure adapts automatically. The artifact mapping in `src/data/artifact-mapping.ts` defines which artifacts each Series produces, and the Engine validates that the expected artifacts are present after each stage. For example, after Stage 3 (Series 2), the Engine checks that 'entities' and 'entity_attributes' artifacts exist in the Session. The natural progression from definition to analysis to specification is reflected in the export pipeline: `src/export/formatters/` has exporters for each output format (JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML, Prompt), and each exporter walks the artifact tree from root to leaves. The stage count impacts the CLI UX: the progress display in `src/engine/progress.ts` shows 'Series 3 of 7 — Round 2 of 4 — Question 3 of 5' giving the user three levels of progress granularity.
variants.strategist: The 8-stage structure is the product's architecture — it defines how users experience SPACE. The definition stage (<1 second) provides instant gratification: the user sees their project created immediately. The interaction stage (2-3 hours) is the core value delivery: each Series completion produces tangible artifacts that the user can review. The export stage (<10 seconds) provides closure: the user gets their specification files. This 3-phase structure mirrors successful product patterns: setup → work → deliver. From a user research perspective, the critical question is whether 7 Series is the right granularity. Too few Series (e.g., 3) would make each Series too long and overwhelming. Too many Series (e.g., 12) would create too many context switches and slow the overall pace. The 7-Series structure was likely chosen because it maps to the 7 categories of a standard software specification document, which is the mental model the target audience (developers) already has. The stage count also impacts the feature roadmap: each stage is a potential entry point for new features. For example, Series 1 (Vision) could add AI-powered question generation, Series 3 (Relationships) could add a visual graph editor, Series 5 (Infrastructure) could add cloud provider integration. The stage decomposition makes it easy to scope and ship individual features without affecting the overall procedure. The key risk is that the 8-stage structure feels rigid — users might want to skip Series 6 (Team) if they're a solo developer. The mitigation is to make Series optional based on project type, but this adds complexity to the dependency resolver.
variants.ethicist: The decision to break SPACE's procedure into 5-8 distinct stages carries implications for cognitive load and decision quality. More stages mean smaller, more focused decision points — which is generally better for reducing decision fatigue and improving answer quality. However, the current breakdown (7 Series, each functioning as a stage) may not align with how people actually think about system design. The stage boundaries are defined by topic (concepts, structure, behavior, data, infrastructure, software, performance), but cognitive stages might be better defined by decision type (explore → decide → validate → commit). By structuring stages around topics rather than cognitive processes, SPACE may inadvertently create artificial transitions that interrupt the natural flow of system thinking. There's also a fairness dimension: the number and granularity of stages determines how much time and effort each topic receives. Infrastructure gets its own Series (Stage 5), but what about security, privacy, or accessibility? The stage allocation reflects the framework designer's priorities, not necessarily the user's. A more equitable breakdown might allocate stages based on project type — an embedded systems project might need 4 stages of infrastructure work and 2 of conceptual work, while a web application might reverse that ratio.
variants.futurist: The 5-8 stage breakdown will dissolve as AI-native specification tools replace fixed-stage procedures with adaptive workflows. Within three years, the number of stages will be dynamic — determined by a pre-flight analysis that examines the project description and recommends a customized question sequence. A simple CRUD application might condense to 3 stages (concept → data model → infrastructure), while a distributed system might expand to 12 stages with dedicated tracks for consistency, fault tolerance, and observability. The stage concept itself will evolve from sequential phases to parallel tracks: future tools will run multiple specification 'threads' simultaneously, where infrastructure questions are answered alongside conceptual questions, and the system cross-references answers across threads in real-time. Within five years, the stage-based procedure will be replaced by a conversational flow where the AI agent asks questions contextually based on what information it still needs, rather than following a predetermined sequence. The explicit stage count will become a configuration option rather than a hard constraint, with power users defining their own stage breakdown and the AI optimizing the question order within each stage.
variants.educator: SPACE's procedure breaks into approximately 5-8 stages, corresponding to the 7 Series in the Framework. Understanding this breakdown helps with planning and time management. For a first-time user, we recommend completing one Series per session to avoid fatigue — that's 7 sessions of 20-30 minutes each. For experienced users working on familiar domains, completing all 7 Series in a single 2-3 hour session is feasible. Each Series maps to a training module: Module 1 covers 'how to think about what your system is,' Module 2 covers 'how to think about its components,' and so on. Build your training materials around these stages, with hands-on exercises for each Series and a capstone exercise that runs through the complete procedure.

text: Where are the key decision points, branches, or conditional paths? At which steps must a choice be made that affects the rest of the flow?

choices.text: No branching — a single linear path from start to finish
Few branches — 1–2 decision points with 2–3 choices each
Moderate branching — multiple decision points with varying path counts

answer:
Decision points and branching:

The primary decision point is the follow-up choice after each open-ended question. Every question has 2-5 follow-up options that classify the answer. This classification drives:
