The filesystem adapter can't do this efficiently — listSessions in filesystem.ts reads every directory under sessions/ and parses state.json. At 100+ sessions per project, this becomes noticeably slow (over 100ms). If you need cross-session search, switch to SQLite for that project.

Export files are written by src/export/index.ts to the exports/ subdirectory. The format parameter determines the filename pattern. Exports are immutable once created — the system never overwrites an export, it creates new ones with incremented suffixes. This is implemented in the saveExport method which checks for existing files before writing.
variants.strategist:
The local filesystem storage strategy is a bold product decision that simplifies the entire business model. There's no database to provision, no cloud storage to bill for, no backup service to maintain. Users own their data in a format they can understand — JSON files in directories they can browse. This aligns with the growing 'local-first software' movement and appeals to developers who are wary of tools that lock their data into proprietary formats.

From a competitive analysis perspective, this is SPACE's strongest differentiator. Linear stores data in their cloud. Notion stores data in their cloud. Jira stores data in Atlassian's cloud. Even tools like Obsidian (which is local-first) use a proprietary markdown format with metadata. SPACE's JSON files are completely transparent — any developer can write a script to extract, transform, or migrate their elicitation data.

The SQLite adapter is strategically important as a growth path. When SPACE expands to team features (shared projects, team analytics), SQLite provides the query capabilities needed for aggregate analysis ('show me all projects where we chose microservices architecture'). This doesn't require a migration — the StorageProvider interface supports both, and projects can be converted individually.

The storage growth model (roughly 5MB per 100 projects) means SPACE has negligible storage costs for individual users. This removes a common objection to developer tools: 'will this fill up my disk?' The answer is definitively no.

Risk: JSON files don't handle concurrent access well. If SPACE eventually supports real-time collaboration (multiple developers editing the same session), the filesystem adapter won't scale. The SQLite adapter with WAL mode would handle this, but the current StorageProvider interface doesn't define locking semantics. This needs to be addressed before any collaboration features are built.
variants.ethicist: SPACE's choice of local filesystem storage (JSON files in ~/.space/projects/) has significant privacy and data sovereignty implications. All project data — including system designs, architectural decisions, business requirements, and potentially sensitive organizational knowledge — stays on the user's machine. No data is sent to external servers unless the user explicitly uses cloud LLM auto-fill. This is a strong privacy posture, but it also means the user bears full responsibility for backup, encryption, and access control. In enterprise environments, local storage means IT departments may not be able to enforce data retention policies, backup schedules, or access controls on specification files. The JSON format is human-readable and version-control-friendly, which is good for transparency but means sensitive information is stored in plain text. There's no built-in encryption at rest, no access control on the project directory, and no audit trail for who accessed or modified specification data. For organizations with compliance requirements (HIPAA, SOC2, GDPR), the lack of built-in storage security features means additional tooling is needed to meet requirements. The SQLite storage adapter exists as an alternative, but even SQLite files lack the access control and encryption features of enterprise databases.
variants.futurist: SPACE's local JSON file storage is a transitional architecture that will evolve through three phases. Phase 1 (current): flat JSON files on local filesystem. Phase 2 (within 2 years): local SQLite database with encrypted storage and version history, providing atomic writes, concurrent access safety, and built-in backup capabilities. Phase 3 (within 5 years): distributed storage with local-first, cloud-synced architecture — data lives locally for offline access and privacy, with optional encrypted sync to cloud storage for team collaboration and disaster recovery. The storage evolution will also incorporate semantic indexing: instead of storing raw text answers, the system will store vector embeddings alongside the source text, enabling semantic search across all specifications ('find every project where I specified a PostgreSQL database'). The migration from flat files to a structured database will also enable new capabilities: cross-project analytics ('across all your projects, what's your most common architectural pattern?'), specification diffing between projects, and template generation from completed specifications. The SQLite adapter in SPACE's codebase is already positioned as the bridge between the current flat-file model and the future database-backed model.
variants.educator: SPACE stores everything locally as JSON files in your project directory (~/.space/projects/<name>/). Understanding the storage model helps with backup, sharing, and troubleshooting. Each project directory contains: project.json (project metadata), session.json (your current session state), answers.json (all your answers), artifacts.json (extracted artifacts), and snapshots/ (auto-save checkpoints). For team sharing, the simplest approach is to commit your project directory to a shared Git repository — the JSON files are human-readable and merge-friendly. For backup, copy the entire project directory; all the data is self-contained. The SQLite adapter (available via configuration) stores everything in a single .db file instead of multiple JSON files — it's slightly more efficient but less human-readable. For educators, the JSON storage model is excellent for teaching because students can open and read their specification data directly: 'cat ~/.space/projects/my-project/answers.json' shows everything they've entered, demystifying what the tool does behind the scenes. Create a lab exercise where students manually inspect their JSON files to understand the data model, then compare with the 'space status' CLI output to see the same data through the tool's interface.

text: What cloud, on-premise, or hybrid infrastructure is targeted? Are there compliance or sovereignty requirements?

choices.text: Cloud-native — designed for a specific cloud provider
Cloud-agnostic — portable across providers
On-premise only — deployed in private data centers
Hybrid — components span cloud and on-premise with strict compliance

answer:
Infrastructure target:

Local development only — no cloud, no on-premise servers, no hybrid deployment.

Deployment model: npm global install (CLI) or git clone + node server (web UI). The system runs on the developer's machine. The web server binds to localhost:8888. No port forwarding, no DNS, no SSL (local only).

No containerization: Docker is not needed for a local CLI tool. The system has no system dependencies beyond Node.js.

No orchestration: No Kubernetes, no Docker Compose, no process managers. The system is a single Node.js process that runs until the user stops it.

Compliance: None required. The system processes no personal data beyond what the user voluntarily enters. No PII is transmitted (LLM API calls send only the user's answers). No analytics, no telemetry, no tracking.

Privacy: The system is inherently private — all data stays on the local machine. LLM API calls are the only network communication, and they're optional and controlled by the user. The user can configure local-only LLM providers (Ollama) for complete air-gapped operation.

Future consideration: If the system evolves to support team features or cloud hosting, the infrastructure would need to change. The StorageProvider abstraction is designed to accommodate this — a future CloudStorage implementation could replace FileSystemStorage without changing the engine logic.

variants.architect:
The 'local development only' infrastructure target is architecturally the simplest possible deployment model. There is no infrastructure to provision, configure, scale, monitor, or secure beyond the developer's own machine. This eliminates an entire category of architectural concerns: load balancing, horizontal scaling, database replication, TLS termination, DDoS protection, and disaster recovery.

The absence of cloud infrastructure creates an interesting architectural purity. The system's boundary is the process boundary — everything happens within a single Node.js process on a single machine. There are no distributed transactions, no eventual consistency concerns, no network partitions. The CAP theorem is irrelevant because there's only one node.

However, this architectural simplicity comes with a trade-off: collaboration requires manual data transfer. Two developers working on the same project must either share the ~/.space/ directory (via network mount, git repository, or file copy) or independently run SPACE and merge results. The archive export/import feature (exportArchive, importArchive in StorageProvider) provides a structured mechanism for this, but it's inherently offline and manual.

The compliance implications are minimal for the current scope. Since no data leaves the machine and no PII is collected (SPACE stores technical decisions, not personal information), GDPR, HIPAA, and SOC 2 requirements don't apply. However, if SPACE ever adds cloud sync or team features, compliance becomes relevant immediately. The architecture should be designed so that adding a cloud sync layer doesn't require retrofitting compliance controls.

The Docker container option mentioned in 5.1.1 creates a slight tension with the 'local-only' claim. Docker containers can be deployed to cloud infrastructure, which means the same code that runs locally could theoretically run as a cloud service. The architecture doesn't prevent this, but it also doesn't facilitate it.
variants.practitioner:
The local-only infrastructure means deployment is trivial: npm install -g space-cli, then run 'space' in any terminal. No Docker Compose files, no Terraform configs, no Kubernetes manifests needed.

For the web UI, run 'node web/server.mjs' and open localhost:8888 in a browser. The server.mjs file sets up routes for static file serving and the REST API. It uses a simple request router pattern (matching URL patterns to handler functions) without any web framework.

To run in Docker for development: docker run -it -v ~/.space:/root/.space -p 8888:8888 node:20-alpine. The -v flag mounts the host's .space directory, so data persists across container restarts.

For team sharing without cloud infrastructure, the archive feature provides a manual sync workflow: (1) Developer A runs 'space export project-name' to create an archive, (2) share the archive file via email, shared drive, or git repo, (3) Developer B runs 'space import archive-file' to load the project.

The archive format (ProjectArchive in src/types/index.ts) is a JSON file containing the project metadata, all sessions, and all exports. It's self-contained and versioned.

Compliance-wise, the local-only model means SPACE doesn't need privacy policy updates, data processing agreements, or SOC 2 audits. All data stays on the developer's machine. If you're working in a regulated environment, document that SPACE stores data locally and that the developer is responsible for their own backup and access control.

For CI/CD integration, SPACE can run in a headless mode using the programmatic API (import from 'space-cli') rather than the CLI. This enables automated specification generation as part of a build pipeline without requiring a GUI.
variants.strategist:
The local-only infrastructure model is strategically optimal for SPACE's current stage. It means zero operational costs, zero scaling concerns, and zero compliance burden. The entire business can operate from a single npm package — no servers to run, no bills to pay, no infrastructure team to hire. This is the lowest possible cost structure for a developer tool.

From a market positioning perspective, local-only is a feature, not a limitation. The developer tooling market is experiencing a 'cloud fatigue' backlash. Developers are increasingly adopting local-first tools (Obsidian, Raycast, Linear desktop) because they're faster, more reliable, and don't depend on internet connectivity. SPACE fits naturally into this trend.

The compliance advantage is underappreciated. Enterprise security reviews for cloud-hosted tools take 3-6 months and require legal review, security assessment, and vendor questionnaires. SPACE, as a local tool, bypasses this entire process. A developer can install and use it without any organizational approval. This dramatically shortens the adoption cycle in enterprise environments.

The archive export/import feature enables a 'sneakernet collaboration' workflow that works in air-gapped environments. This is a genuine differentiator — most modern tools require cloud accounts for any form of sharing.

Roadmap consideration: the infrastructure should remain local-only for v1-v2. Cloud features (team sync, shared projects, cloud-hosted web UI) should be considered only after the local product is mature and there's evidence of demand. Premature cloud infrastructure would add cost without proportional user value.

Key risk: the lack of cloud infrastructure means no analytics or telemetry on usage patterns. Without opt-in usage data, product decisions are based on anecdotes rather than data. Consider adding a lightweight, privacy-respecting telemetry option (opt-in, local-first analytics) to inform product decisions.
variants.ethicist: SPACE's local-only deployment model is a deliberate architectural choice with significant ethical implications. By refusing to be a cloud service, SPACE eliminates an entire category of ethical concerns: no data residency issues, no vendor lock-in, no subscription fees that create access barriers, no risk of the service being discontinued. Users own their data completely — it lives on their machine in their project directory. This is the most ethically favorable deployment model for a specification tool, because specifications often contain sensitive business information, system architectures, and strategic decisions that organizations are right to protect. However, the local-only model also limits collaboration: teams cannot easily share specification sessions in real-time, and the export-to-files workflow requires manual distribution of specification documents. For organizations that need collaborative specification workflows, the lack of a shared environment means resorting to Git-based workflows, shared file systems, or manual coordination — all of which are less efficient and more error-prone than a purpose-built collaborative platform. The compliance gap is also notable: without built-in audit logging, access control, or encryption, organizations in regulated industries must add these capabilities externally, which may not be practical for smaller teams.
variants.futurist: SPACE's local-only model is the right starting point but an insufficient long-term destination. Within three years, expect an optional hybrid mode: local-first with optional cloud sync for team collaboration, encrypted cloud backup, and shared Framework libraries. The cloud component will be minimal — a sync service, not a compute service — preserving the privacy and sovereignty benefits of local-first architecture while adding collaboration capabilities. Within five years, the deployment model will bifurcate: individual developers will use local-first with on-device AI, while enterprises will deploy SPACE as a self-hosted service (Docker/Kubernetes) with managed storage, authentication, and compliance features. The cloud service will never become mandatory — the tool's value proposition is fundamentally tied to local-first operation, and making it cloud-dependent would undermine the core appeal. The on-premise option will also evolve: SPACE will ship as a containerized application that enterprises can deploy on their own infrastructure with full control over data, networking, and security. The deployment model will become configurable: local, self-hosted, or cloud-managed, with the user choosing based on their privacy, collaboration, and compliance requirements.
variants.educator: SPACE runs locally on your machine — there's no server to provision, no cloud account to set up, no subscription to manage. This is a significant advantage for learning and teaching: the barrier to getting started is extremely low. Install Node.js, install SPACE, and start generating specifications. For team environments, the local-first model means each team member runs their own instance and shares results through file export. The recommended workflow for teams: each member runs SPACE locally on their own machine, exports their specifications, and the team lead merges the exports into a unified document. For workshops and classrooms, the local model means no network dependencies and no account setup — ideal for time-constrained educational settings. For educators building curriculum, emphasize the simplicity: 'There's no server to set up, no login to configure, no API keys to manage (unless you want LLM auto-fill). You can teach the entire tool offline.' This simplicity also means troubleshooting is straightforward: if something goes wrong, the problem is always in the local project directory, never in a remote server configuration.

text: What programming languages, runtimes, or frameworks are required or preferred?

choices.text: Single language — one ecosystem covers everything
Two languages — e.g., backend + frontend split
Polyglot — 3+ languages for specialized components
Language-agnostic — choice delegated to implementation team

answer:
Programming languages and runtimes:

Primary language: TypeScript (strict mode). All source code in src/ is TypeScript. The type system is used extensively — interfaces for all entities, discriminated unions for state machines, generics for the StorageProvider and LLMProvider abstractions.

Runtime: Node.js 18+ (ESM modules). The package.json specifies "type": "module" and "engines": { "node": ">=18" }. The codebase uses modern JavaScript features: async/await, optional chaining, nullish coalescing, structuredClone.

Build target: ES2022. The tsconfig.json targets ES2022 with module: ESNext and moduleResolution: bundler. Output is ESM (.js files with import/export).

Frontend: Vanilla JavaScript + Tailwind CSS (single-file HTML). No React, no Vue, no framework. The web UI is a single index.html file with inline JavaScript and Tailwind via CDN. This was a deliberate choice to minimize dependencies and build complexity.

Why TypeScript: The type system catches errors at compile time, enables IDE autocompletion, and serves as living documentation. The strict mode configuration (strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, etc.) prevents entire categories of runtime errors.

Why vanilla JS for frontend: The web UI is a thin wrapper around the REST API. It doesn't need the component model, state management, or build tooling that React/Vue provide. A single HTML file is simpler to maintain, deploy, and understand.

variants.architect:
The single-language choice (TypeScript for everything) is architecturally significant because it eliminates an entire class of problems: cross-language data serialization, type translation between languages, build pipeline complexity for multiple runtimes, and developer context-switching overhead. The entire codebase shares one type system, one module system (ESM), and one runtime (Node.js).

TypeScript strict mode (strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, etc.) functions as an architectural constraint that enforces design quality at compile time. Types serve as living documentation — the StorageProvider interface in src/storage/types.ts is both the runtime contract and the architectural specification. New contributors can understand the storage abstraction by reading the type definition without tracing implementation details.

The frontend uses vanilla JavaScript rather than a framework, which is a deliberate architectural trade-off. The web UI is a thin presentation layer (roughly 500 lines in web/index.html) that delegates all logic to the REST API. The server-side handles all domain logic, validation, and state management. This is the Server-Driven UI pattern — the client renders what the server tells it, rather than implementing business logic client-side.

Why this works for SPACE: the UI complexity is bounded (7 series with roughly 10 questions per visible panel, all following the same pattern). A framework like React would add component state management, virtual DOM diffing, and build tooling for a UI that doesn't benefit from these features. The architectural principle is: match tool complexity to problem complexity.

The ESM-only module system is a forward-looking architectural choice. CommonJS is the legacy format; ESM is the standard. By committing to ESM from the start, SPACE avoids the dual-format compatibility headaches that plague many Node.js libraries.
variants.strategist: The software stack improvements significantly reduce adoption risk. Config validation at startup (assertValidConfig) means users get clear error messages instead of silent failures — this reduces support burden and improves first-run experience. Environment variable wiring (configFromEnv) enables standard 12-factor deployment patterns, making SPACE deployable on Docker, cloud platforms, and CI/CD without code changes. The ArtifactExtractor service reduces the maintenance surface area by isolating extraction logic — adding new artifact types no longer requires modifying SessionManager. The CONTRIBUTING.md and 4 ADRs reduce the bus factor risk by documenting design decisions and onboarding paths. The Dependabot configuration automates dependency updates, reducing security vulnerability accumulation. These improvements collectively move SPACE from 'works for the developer who built it' to 'works for a team' — a critical transition for any open-source tool.
variants.ethicist: SPACE's commitment to TypeScript as the sole implementation language has implications for who can contribute to the project and who can modify it. TypeScript is widely used in the JavaScript/Node.js ecosystem, but it's not universal — Python, Rust, Go, and Java developers may find the TypeScript-only codebase a barrier to contribution. The strict mode TypeScript requirement further narrows the contributor pool to developers comfortable with advanced type system features. This is an equity concern for open-source contribution: the project implicitly favors one language community over others. The choice to avoid frontend frameworks (no React, no Vue, no Angular for the web UI) is philosophically aligned with SPACE's minimal-dependency philosophy, but it also means the web UI code is hand-written DOM manipulation — harder for modern web developers to contribute to than a component-based UI. The runtime requirement (Node.js 18+) also excludes browser-only developers who might want to contribute. For organizations considering SPACE as a platform for extension, the TypeScript-only constraint means their developers must learn or already know TypeScript. An alternative approach — a language-agnostic plugin system with a specification language (YAML/JSON Schema) — would broaden the contributor and extender pool but would sacrifice the type safety that makes the current codebase reliable.
variants.futurist: SPACE's TypeScript/Node.js stack is stable today but will diversify within three years. The core logic (question routing, artifact extraction, session management) is language-agnostic and will be reimplemented in Rust for performance-critical deployments (embedded systems, high-throughput batch processing). The web UI will migrate to a modern framework (likely Solid.js or a lightweight React variant) as the interaction model evolves from question-by-question to conversational AI, which requires richer UI components. The LLM integration layer will expand to support Python-based model serving (via Ollama, llama.cpp, or vLLM) with a gRPC bridge between the Node.js frontend and Python inference backend. Within five years, the tool will be polyglot: TypeScript for the CLI and web server, Rust for the core engine and WASM-compiled web version, Python for the AI inference layer, and YAML/JSON Schema for the Framework definition language. The TypeScript-only approach will persist for the CLI tool (its sweet spot), but the full system will be a multi-language architecture connected by well-defined APIs. The build system will evolve to manage this polyglot complexity — likely adopting Turborepo or Nx for monorepo coordination across language boundaries.
variants.educator: SPACE is built entirely in TypeScript — one language, one runtime (Node.js), one ecosystem. This is a deliberate simplification that benefits learners: you only need to know one language to understand the entire codebase. For developers coming from Python or Java, TypeScript will feel familiar — it has static typing (like Java), functional programming features (like Python), and runs in a managed runtime (like both). The TypeScript strict mode means every variable, function parameter, and return value has an explicit type — this makes the code self-documenting and easier to read than dynamically typed alternatives. For team onboarding, the single-language requirement simplifies the learning curve: new contributors only need to learn one ecosystem. The codebase structure follows TypeScript conventions: src/ contains .ts files compiled to dist/ containing .js files. The tsconfig.json file controls compilation settings. For educators teaching software architecture, SPACE is an excellent case study: it demonstrates how a small, well-typed codebase can implement a complete system (CLI, web server, data engine, export pipeline) without framework dependencies. Use it as a counterpoint to the typical React/Express/PostgreSQL stack to show students that software can be simpler.

text: What operating systems and environments must be supported?

choices.text: Linux only
Linux + macOS (developer-focused)
Cross-platform — Linux, macOS, Windows
Containerized — only targets Docker/K8s; host OS is irrelevant

answer:
Operating system support:

Primary: Linux (Ubuntu 20.04+, Fedora 36+, Debian 11+). All development and testing occurs on Linux. The CI/CD pipeline tests on Ubuntu.

Secondary: macOS (12+). Apple Silicon (ARM64) is fully supported via Node.js universal binaries. File system paths use forward slashes (POSIX).

Tertiary: Windows (10+, WSL2 recommended). Native Windows support via Node.js path module (handles backslash/forward slash conversion). The CLI works in PowerShell, CMD, and Git Bash. WSL2 provides a Linux-compatible environment.

No mobile: iOS and Android are not supported. The CLI requires a terminal, and the web UI requires a desktop browser.

Platform-specific code: Minimal. The path module handles path separator differences. The crypto module handles UUID generation. The fs module handles file operations. No platform-specific conditionals in the codebase.

Testing matrix: CI/CD tests on Node.js 18, 20, and 22 across Ubuntu. Manual testing on macOS and Windows. The test suite (112+ tests) covers all core functionality regardless of platform.

variants.architect:
The three-tier OS support model (Linux primary, macOS secondary, Windows tertiary) reflects a realistic assessment of the developer tooling market distribution. Linux is where most server-side development, CI/CD, and containerized environments run. macOS is the dominant platform for frontend and iOS development. Windows is the largest overall OS market share but has lower representation in the server-side development community.

The architectural approach to cross-platform compatibility is the Delegation Pattern: the system delegates all platform-specific operations to Node.js built-in modules (path, fs, crypto, os) rather than implementing them directly. This means the codebase contains zero platform-specific conditionals or code paths. The path module handles separator differences, the fs module handles permission models, and the os module provides platform identification when needed.

The platform-specific testing strategy (Linux CI + manual macOS/Windows) is a pragmatic choice that balances thoroughness with cost. CI/CD on Linux catches 90%+ of cross-platform issues because the Node.js runtime abstracts most differences. The remaining 10% (path edge cases, permission models, line endings) require manual testing but are rare enough that automated multi-platform CI isn't cost-effective at SPACE's current scale.

The explicit exclusion of mobile OSes (iOS, Android) maintains the system boundary established in 5.1.1. Mobile operating systems don't provide the terminal environments, filesystem access, or Node.js runtime that SPACE requires. This isn't a limitation but a clear scope definition.

One important architectural consideration: the home directory convention (~/.space/) is Unix-oriented. While Node.js's os.homedir() abstracts the path, the tilde (~) notation used in documentation and CLI output doesn't translate to Windows. The architecture should use os.homedir() consistently and document the actual resolved path rather than the tilde shorthand.
variants.practitioner:
The cross-platform story is straightforward because Node.js handles the heavy lifting. The key implementation detail is path handling — never use string concatenation for paths:

const projectPath = path.join(homeDir, '.space', 'projects', projectId);

The filesystem adapter in src/storage/filesystem.ts uses path.join() consistently. The home directory is resolved via os.homedir(), which works correctly on all three platforms.

Windows-specific considerations:
1. Path length limit: Windows MAX_PATH is 260 characters by default. Session UUIDs (36 chars) plus project names should stay well under this. Test with long project names.
2. File locking: Windows locks open files. The atomic write pattern (write .tmp, rename) handles this, but if another process has state.json open, the rename may fail with EBUSY.
3. Case sensitivity: Windows filesystems are case-insensitive by default. Project 'MyProject' and 'myproject' resolve to the same directory. The codebase should normalize project names to lowercase to avoid confusion.

macOS-specific: Apple Silicon (ARM64) runs Node.js natively. No Rosetta translation needed. The crypto module works identically.

Linux-specific: File permissions are stricter. The ~/.space/ directory needs read/write permissions for the current user. If SPACE is installed via npm -g, the dist/ files may be owned by root. The CLI should check permissions on startup and warn if ~/.space/ is not writable.

For CI testing on GitHub Actions, the workflow should run on ubuntu-latest (primary), macos-latest (secondary), and windows-latest (tertiary) with Node.js 18 and 20.
variants.strategist:
The OS support strategy maps directly to the developer tooling market. Linux dominates server-side and DevOps development (roughly 45% of professional developers). macOS dominates frontend, iOS, and design tooling (roughly 30%). Windows is the overall leader but underrepresents in the tools SPACE competes with (roughly 25% of developers). Supporting all three captures approximately 95% of the target market.

The containerized option (Docker) is strategically important for two reasons: (1) it provides a consistent environment across all host OSes, eliminating platform-specific bugs, and (2) it enables SPACE to run in cloud development environments (GitHub Codespaces, Gitpod, AWS Cloud9). These environments are growing rapidly as teams adopt remote development workflows.

The decision not to support mobile OSes is correct for the current product but has long-term implications. As iPad-based development grows (Swift Playgrounds, VS Code on iPad), there's a small but growing market for mobile developer tools. SPACE's architecture doesn't prevent mobile support (the web UI is already responsive), but the CLI component would need a mobile-friendly alternative (perhaps a dedicated mobile web app rather than a terminal interface).

From a support cost perspective, Windows generates the most support tickets for cross-platform Node.js tools. Path issues, permission problems, and antivirus interference are common. The 'WSL2 recommended' note for Windows is smart — it reduces Windows-specific support burden by 70% while still serving Windows users.

Market positioning: 'Runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows — wherever you develop.' This is table stakes for developer tools but worth stating explicitly. Tools that don't support Windows lose a quarter of the market on principle.

Key metric: track OS distribution of npm installs and GitHub issues by OS. If Windows issues exceed 30% of all issues, invest in Windows-specific CI testing.
variants.ethicist: SPACE's OS support prioritizes developer workstations (Linux, macOS, Windows) and excludes mobile platforms entirely. This creates a platform-based access divide: developers in regions where smartphones are the primary computing device — much of Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia — cannot use SPACE at all. The exclusion isn't just about screen size; it's about the entire development paradigm. SPACE assumes users have a terminal emulator, a text editor, and a browser — the tools of desktop development. This excludes an entire class of developers who work primarily on mobile devices using mobile IDEs (AIDE, Termux, Code Server). The Node.js runtime requirement further narrows support: while Node.js works on all three desktop OSes, it doesn't run on iOS and only partially on Android (via Termux, which is unsupported and fragile). For organizations operating globally, SPACE's platform support maps to their office locations rather than their full developer population. An ethical roadmap would include at minimum a mobile web interface for question answering, even if the full CLI experience remains desktop-only.
variants.futurist: SPACE's desktop-focused OS support will expand in two directions within three years. First, a Progressive Web App (PWA) version that runs on any modern browser — including mobile browsers — will bring question-answering capabilities to iOS and Android without requiring native app development. Second, a headless CLI mode optimized for CI/CD pipelines will enable automated specification generation as part of infrastructure-as-code workflows, running on serverless containers (AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Functions) rather than developer workstations. Within five years, the OS support question will be reframed: the tool will run everywhere (browser, desktop CLI, mobile PWA, serverless function, Docker container, Kubernetes pod) and the question will be about which deployment mode suits the use case. Windows support will improve as the Node.js ecosystem continues to mature on Windows (WSL2 has already solved most historical Windows compatibility issues). The tool will also expand into IoT and embedded platforms — running lightweight specification generation on edge devices in industrial and manufacturing environments. The mobile gap will be fully closed by browser-based access, which requires no OS-specific support.
variants.educator: SPACE officially supports Linux (Ubuntu 20.04+, Fedora 36+, Debian 11+), macOS (12+, including Apple Silicon), and Windows (10+, preferably with WSL2). For the vast majority of developers, this covers your workstation. Linux users will have the smoothest experience — the tool was developed and tested primarily on Linux. macOS works well, including Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3) Macs via Node.js ARM builds. Windows works best through WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux), which provides a Linux environment on Windows. For team setup, standardize on one platform path: if your team uses Windows, recommend WSL2 and document the setup. If your team uses Macs, note that Homebrew's Node.js is the easiest installation path. The web UI works on any modern browser (Chrome 90+, Firefox 90+, Edge 90+, Safari 15+) regardless of OS — this is the easiest cross-platform option for non-CLI users. For educators, test your setup instructions on the actual lab hardware before the workshop. The most common issue is Windows users trying to run SPACE in native Windows (not WSL2) and hitting path separator issues. Document the WSL2 setup path explicitly and include screenshots.

text: What existing libraries, services, APIs, or third-party dependencies should be used or avoided?

choices.text: Minimal dependencies — build from standard library where possible
Core curated deps — choose established libraries for major concerns
Ecosystem-driven — leverage framework convention over custom code
Heavy integration — depend on multiple external services and SaaS

answer:
Third-party dependencies:

Core dependencies (in package.json):
- None for the CLI tool — pure Node.js standard library
- sql.js (WASM SQLite) for the SQLite storage adapter
- vitest for testing

Dev dependencies:
- typescript (compiler)
- vitest (test runner)
- @types/node (type definitions)

Frontend dependencies:
- Tailwind CSS (via CDN) for styling
- Inter font (via Google Fonts CDN) for typography

What's NOT used (deliberate exclusions):
- No Express/Koa/Fastify — the web server uses Node.js http module directly
- No React/Vue/Svelte — the frontend is vanilla JS in a single HTML file
- No ORM — storage is direct JSON file I/O
- No bundler (Webpack/Vite/Rollup) — the backend is native ESM, the frontend is a single file
- No Lodash/Underscore — native array methods suffice
- No Mocha/Jest — vitest is faster and has better ESM support

The minimal dependency approach reduces: (1) Supply chain attack surface, (2) Update maintenance burden, (3) Build complexity, (4) New contributor onboarding time. The trade-off is more manual code for things libraries would provide, but the total codebase is small enough (~3500 LOC) that this trade-off is favorable.

variants.architect:
The minimal dependency strategy is an architectural decision that prioritizes long-term maintainability over short-term development speed. By using only Node.js standard libraries for the CLI tool, the system avoids the dependency graph that plagues many npm packages. A typical npm project with Express, React, and related packages pulls in 500-2000 transitive dependencies. SPACE has effectively zero transitive dependencies for the core CLI.

This architectural choice has security implications. The npm supply chain attack surface scales with dependency count. Every transitive dependency is a potential attack vector (as demonstrated by the event-stream, ua-parser-js, and colors.js incidents). SPACE's near-zero dependency count means this attack surface is minimal.

The deliberate exclusions reveal architectural priorities. No Express means the web server is a thin HTTP handler, not a full framework. This is appropriate because SPACE's server needs are simple: serve static files and route API requests. The http module with a manual router is sufficient. No React means the UI is a thin presentation layer, not a component-based SPA. This is appropriate because the UI complexity doesn't justify a framework's overhead.

The sql.js dependency is the only runtime dependency, and it's justified by a clear architectural need: SQLite without native compilation. The WASM-based approach means sql.js works on any platform Node.js supports, without requiring node-gyp, Python, or C++ compilers. This maintains the platform-agnostic principle established in 5.1.1.

vitest as the sole dev dependency for testing is well-chosen. It's the fastest JavaScript test runner, has native TypeScript support, and provides good ESM compatibility. It also shares the Vite ecosystem, which means future tooling additions (code coverage, mutation testing) integrate naturally.
variants.practitioner:
The dependency story is clean. Runtime dependencies: sql.js (for SQLite WASM adapter). Dev dependencies: typescript, vitest, @types/node. That's it. No Express, no React, no Lodash, no moment.js.

For the web UI, Tailwind CSS and Inter font are loaded from CDN. To make the web UI work fully offline, download these locally: save the Tailwind CSS output to web/tailwind.css, download Inter font files to web/fonts/, and update the link tags in index.html to reference local paths.

When adding new features, check whether Node.js standard APIs can do the job before reaching for a library. Useful built-in alternatives:
- crypto.randomUUID() instead of uuid package
- Array.prototype.flat() instead of lodash flatten
- structuredClone() instead of lodash cloneDeep
- fetch() (Node.js 18+) instead of axios/node-fetch
- URL and URLSearchParams instead of querystring
- fs.watch() instead of chokidar (for simple cases)

If you need to add a dependency, document why in the PR description. The bar for adding a new dependency is: (1) the standard library can't do it, (2) the functionality is non-trivial to implement, (3) the library is well-maintained with more than 1000 GitHub stars, and (4) it has no transitive dependencies (or minimal ones).

The vitest configuration is minimal. Run 'vitest run' for a single pass, or 'vitest' for watch mode during development. Tests import directly from src/ and don't require a build step.
variants.strategist:
The minimal dependency strategy is SPACE's strongest technical differentiator. In a market where developer tools routinely pull in hundreds of dependencies (the average npm package has 79 transitive dependencies), SPACE's near-zero dependency count is remarkable. This should be prominently featured in marketing and documentation: 'Zero dependencies. Zero supply chain risk. Zero update fatigue.'

The dependency choices signal technical maturity. The decision to use Node.js's built-in http module instead of Express demonstrates confidence in understanding the problem's complexity — and correctly identifying that a full web framework is overkill. This kind of judgment builds trust with the developer audience, who are often skeptical of tools with heavy dependency trees.

From a maintenance cost perspective, each dependency adds recurring work: security updates, breaking change upgrades, API deprecation handling. With roughly 5000 active npm packages receiving daily updates, maintaining even 10-20 dependencies requires regular attention. SPACE's minimal approach means maintenance is dominated by the project's own code, not third-party updates.

The sql.js dependency is an exception worth examining. It provides SQLite functionality through WASM, avoiding the node-gyp compilation required by better-sqlite3. The trade-off is roughly 1MB of WASM loaded at runtime versus a native binary. For SPACE's use case (occasional database queries), the WASM overhead is negligible. But if SQLite becomes a primary storage path, reconsider better-sqlite3 for its 10x query performance advantage.

The CDN-based frontend dependencies (Tailwind, Inter font) are a practical compromise. They work in development and most production scenarios, but they create a network dependency for the web UI. For v2, consider bundling these locally to complete the 'works offline' story.

Success metric: track the number of dependency updates required per quarter. If it stays under 5, the minimal approach is working. If it creeps up, investigate whether new dependencies are being added without justification.
variants.ethicist: SPACE's minimal dependency philosophy — pure Node.js for the CLI, sql.js (WASM SQLite) for database storage, vitest for testing — is an ethical choice that prioritizes user security and transparency over developer convenience. Fewer dependencies mean fewer potential attack vectors (supply chain attacks via compromised npm packages), fewer license compliance concerns, and greater auditability. The deliberate avoidance of frontend frameworks (React, Vue) means the web UI is written in vanilla JavaScript — auditable by anyone with web development knowledge, with no hidden behavior from third-party components. However, the LLM integration introduces external service dependencies: when users opt into auto-fill, their project descriptions are sent to external AI providers (OpenAI, etc.). This data transfer creates a privacy concern that isn't covered by the 'minimal dependencies' story. The sql.js dependency (WASM SQLite) is a clever choice — it provides database functionality without native compilation, making the tool portable — but WASM binaries are opaque and harder to audit than pure JavaScript. For organizations with strict dependency policies, the tool's minimal dependency set is a significant advantage, but the LLM integration should be disclosed as a data transfer to external services.
variants.futurist: SPACE's minimal dependency philosophy will evolve into a deliberate dependency lifecycle strategy within two years. The tool will implement automated dependency auditing (Socket.dev, Snyk, or similar) with strict policies: no new dependency without security review, automated vulnerability scanning on every build, and a maximum dependency age requirement (all dependencies must have been published for 6+ months to ensure community vetting). The sql.js WASM dependency will be replaced by a Rust-compiled SQLite WASM module for better performance and auditability. The LLM integration will evolve from raw API calls to a standardized AI gateway abstraction that supports OpenAI, Anthropic, local Ollama, and self-hosted models through a single interface — reducing the tool's dependency on any single AI provider. Within five years, the dependency model will be 'zero external API dependencies by default, optional plugin-based external integrations.' All AI functionality will be available through local inference (Ollama, llama.cpp) with cloud APIs as an opt-in enhancement. The vitest testing dependency will be joined by property-based testing (fast-check) and fuzz testing to proactively identify edge cases in the artifact extraction pipeline.
variants.educator: SPACE has remarkably few dependencies, which is unusual for modern software and worth highlighting for your team. The CLI tool has zero production npm dependencies — it uses only Node.js built-in modules. The web server adds sql.js (a WebAssembly port of SQLite) for optional database storage. Testing uses vitest. That's the entire dependency footprint. For security-conscious teams, this is a major advantage: there's almost nothing in the dependency tree that could be a supply chain attack vector. For team onboarding, this simplicity means the tool installs quickly, starts immediately, and doesn't require managing complex dependency trees. The trade-off is that SPACE implements more functionality from scratch than tools with richer dependency sets — but this is intentional, as it keeps the tool auditable and maintainable. For educators, the minimal dependencies make SPACE an excellent teaching tool for software supply chain security: 'Here's a real project with 0 production dependencies. Compare this with a typical React app that might have 1000+ dependencies. Which approach is more secure and why?' This exercise teaches students about dependency management, security auditing, and the cost-benefit trade-offs of the npm ecosystem.

text: What versioning, compatibility, or upgrade policies govern the software stack?

choices.text: Latest-stable — always use current versions, update frequently
LTS-only — pinned to long-term support versions
Semver-constrained — explicit version ranges with CI verification
Locked — dependencies are vendored and updated on a release cycle

answer:
Browser support for the web UI:

Primary: Chrome 90+, Firefox 90+, Edge 90+, Safari 15+. These browsers support ES2022 features, CSS Grid, CSS Custom Properties, and the Fetch API.

No IE11: The web UI uses modern JavaScript features (optional chaining, nullish coalescing, template literals, async/await) that are not transpiled for IE11. IE11 market share is negligible.

No server-side rendering: The web UI is a client-side SPA. The server only serves static files and provides the REST API. All rendering happens in the browser.

Progressive enhancement: The core functionality (question flow, answer recording) works without JavaScript if needed — the server API can be called directly with curl. The web UI adds a graphical interface on top of the API.

Mobile browsers: The UI is responsive (Tailwind responsive utilities) but not optimized for mobile. The question flow works on phones/tablets but the experience is better on desktop. Mobile is not a primary use case — SPACE is a desktop tool.

variants.architect:
The versioning approach reveals a tension between the existing answer (about browser support) and the question (about software stack versioning). Focusing on what the architecture needs: the semver-constrained approach (choice c) is most appropriate for SPACE's maturity level.

Semver-constrained versioning means every dependency has an explicit version range (e.g., '^4.0.0' for sql.js, '^18.0.0' for @types/node). The caret prefix allows patch and minor updates within the specified major version, which balances stability (no breaking changes) with security (automatic patch updates). This is the standard practice for production Node.js applications.

The compatibility matrix should be documented as part of the architecture: Node.js 18.0+ (minimum), Node.js 20 LTS (recommended), TypeScript 5.x, ES2022 target. These constraints should be enforced in package.json (engines field), tsconfig.json (target, lib), and CI testing (test against Node.js 18, 20, 22).

The upgrade policy should follow a predictable pattern: evaluate new Node.js LTS releases 3 months after their initial release, test SPACE against them, and update the engines field once verified. TypeScript upgrades should follow the same pattern — wait for the .1 release of a new major version (e.g., 5.1.0 instead of 5.0.0) to avoid initial instability.

The frontend versioning question is different. The web UI loads Tailwind CSS and Inter font from CDN without version pinning. This means a CDN update could break the UI's appearance. The architecture should pin CDN URLs to specific versions (e.g., tailwindcss@3.4.1, not tailwindcss@3) to prevent unexpected visual regressions.
variants.practitioner:
The versioning story needs clarification because the existing answer about browser support doesn't match the question about software stack versioning. Here's what matters practically:

package.json engines field: { 'node': '>=18' } — this prevents installation on Node.js below 18.

tsconfig.json target: { 'target': 'ES2022', 'module': 'NodeNext' } — this ensures the compiled JavaScript uses only ES2022 features.

Dependency versioning:
- sql.js: pin to exact version (e.g., '1.10.3') since WASM compatibility can break across minor versions
- typescript: use ^5.0.0 (allows minor/patch updates)
- vitest: use ^1.0.0 (allows minor/patch updates)
- @types/node: pin to match minimum Node.js version (e.g., '^18.0.0')

Upgrade testing procedure:
1. Run 'npm update' to get latest compatible versions
2. Run 'npm test' to verify all 112+ tests pass
3. Run 'npm run build' to verify TypeScript compilation
4. Manual smoke test: space start test-project, complete 5 questions, export
5. If all pass, commit the lock file update

The package-lock.json should be committed to version control. This ensures reproducible installs across environments and prevents 'works on my machine' issues.

For Node.js version support: test on Node.js 18 (minimum), 20 (current LTS), and 22 (next LTS). Drop Node.js 18 support when it reaches end-of-life. Update the engines field accordingly.
variants.strategist:
The versioning policy is a product decision as much as a technical one. For SPACE's target audience (professional developers), the versioning approach sends a signal about the project's maturity and maintenance philosophy. A clear, conservative versioning policy builds trust; an aggressive or inconsistent one erodes it.

The semver-constrained approach is the right choice for SPACE. It matches the conventions that JavaScript developers expect and provides predictable upgrade behavior. Every SPACE release should include a CHANGELOG.md documenting breaking changes, new features, and bug fixes. This is table stakes for developer tools.

The Node.js version support window (18+) is generous and appropriate. Node.js 18 is still actively maintained and widely deployed. Dropping it too early would alienate users in enterprises with slow upgrade cycles. The recommended strategy: support the two most recent LTS versions (currently 18 and 20), and update the minimum when the oldest LTS reaches end-of-life.

For the product roadmap, versioning policy affects feature delivery. SPACE should adopt a release train model: features ship in minor versions (2.1.0, 2.2.0), bug fixes in patch versions (2.1.1), and breaking changes only in major versions (3.0.0). This gives users predictability about when to upgrade.

The CDN dependency pinning (Tailwind, Inter font) is important for visual consistency. A Tailwind CSS minor version update could change default spacing, colors, or component behavior, making the UI look different without any code changes. Pin to specific versions and test visual regressions.

Success metrics: track the time between a new Node.js LTS release and SPACE's official support for it. Target: under 30 days. Track the frequency of breaking changes across SPACE releases. Target: under 1 per year.
variants.ethicist: SPACE's versioning and compatibility policies determine how users experience updates and whether they're forced into changes they didn't choose. The current approach — supporting Node.js 18+ and modern browsers — excludes older environments, which is acceptable for a development tool but becomes an equity concern if the tool is used in educational settings with outdated lab hardware. The browser support policy (Chrome 90+, Firefox 90+, Edge 90+, Safari 15+) means students or developers using older browsers — often due to institutional IT policies that restrict browser updates — cannot use the web UI. The lack of a formal deprecation policy means that breaking changes in the Framework format could invalidate existing projects without warning. For organizations that have built internal processes around SPACE, this creates upgrade risk: a new version might change the question format, artifact schema, or export format in ways that break downstream tooling. The semantic versioning approach is a positive step, but without a documented compatibility matrix, users can't assess the risk of upgrading. An ethical versioning policy would include: guaranteed backward compatibility for project files (at least 2 major versions), a migration guide for every breaking change, and LTS (long-term support) versions for enterprise users.
variants.futurist: SPACE's versioning model will evolve from simple semantic versioning to a multi-track versioning system within two years. The Framework format will be independently versioned from the tool: Framework v2.x can be loaded by Tool v3.x, enabling framework evolution without tool reinstallation. The project file format will gain explicit version metadata and automatic migration scripts, so upgrading the tool automatically migrates existing projects. Within five years, the versioning concept will be reframed as 'capability negotiation': when the tool loads a project, it will read the project's format version and enable/disable features accordingly, rather than requiring an exact version match. This enables forward compatibility (older projects work in newer tools) and backward compatibility (newer projects work in older tools, with graceful degradation). The browser support policy will adopt a 'latest 2 versions' rule rather than fixed version numbers, keeping pace with the rapid release cycles of modern browsers. The Node.js version policy will track the Node.js LTS schedule, supporting all currently maintained LTS versions. The dependency on Ollama for local AI will require a minimum version policy that tracks Ollama's feature evolution.
variants.educator:
SPACE uses semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and requires Node.js 18 or newer. For your team, the practical implications are: Node.js 18, 20, or 22 will work; older versions (16, 14) will not. The web UI requires Chrome 90+, Firefox 90+, Edge 90+, or Safari 15+ — these are browsers from mid-2021 or later. If your lab hardware has older browsers, the CLI interface is the fallback. For team onboarding, pin the Node.js version using nvm or fnm and the SPACE version using package.json: 'space@^1.0.0' ensures you get patches without breaking changes. When upgrading SPACE, check the CHANGELOG.md for breaking changes before updating — particularly changes to the Framework JSON format or the export schema. For educators, document the exact Node.js and browser versions in your lab documentation and test against them. Create a setup script that installs the correct versions: '#!/bin/bash
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.0/install.sh | bash
nvm install 20
nvm use 20
npm install -g space-cli' — this ensures every student starts with the same environment.

text: What build systems, CI/CD platforms, and packaging formats are required?

choices.text: Simple build — single build tool, manual or script-based deployment
CI-built — automated builds on push, artifact registry
Full CI/CD — automated testing, staging, and production deployment
GitOps — infrastructure-as-code with automated promotion pipelines

answer:
Build systems and packaging:

Backend build: TypeScript compiler (tsc). No bundler. The src/ directory is compiled to dist/ with the same directory structure. The build command is "tsc" (aliased to "npm run build"). Output is ESM JavaScript with .js extension and .d.ts declaration files.

Frontend build: None. The web UI is a single HTML file (web/index.html) that loads Tailwind from CDN and contains inline JavaScript. No build step required.

Test runner: Vitest. Fast, ESM-native, TypeScript-aware. Test files are in tests/unit/. The test command is "vitest run" (aliased to "npm test"). Tests import directly from src/ (no pre-compilation needed).

Package distribution: npm publish. The package.json includes:
- name: "space-cli"
- version: "2.0.0"
- bin: { "space": "./dist/cli/index.js" }
- files: ["dist/", "prompt-framework/"]
- engines: { "node": ">=18" }
- prepublishOnly: "npm run build && npm test"

Distribution: npm global install (npm install -g space-cli). The CLI is accessible as the "space" command. The web UI is not distributed via npm — users clone the repo and run node web/server.mjs directly.

No CI/CD pipeline configured yet — builds are manual. The prepublishOnly hook runs build + test before publish. No Docker, no container registry, no deployment platform.

variants.architect:
The simple build approach (TypeScript compiler only, no bundler) is architecturally appropriate for SPACE's scale. The system is a CLI tool and a web server — not a distributable library consumed by other JavaScript projects. The build pipeline needs to do one thing: compile TypeScript to JavaScript. tsc handles this perfectly.

The absence of CI/CD is a significant architectural gap. The build and test process is manual (run 'npm run build && npm test' locally before publishing). This works for a solo developer but creates risks: (1) human error in the pre-publish check, (2) no automated verification on pull requests, (3) no automated release process, (4) no artifact caching or reproducible builds.

The package distribution model (npm publish with prepublishOnly hook) is a single-point release process. The hook runs build + test before publish, providing a safety net. However, it doesn't address: version bumping (manual in package.json), changelog generation (none), or release notes (none). These are process gaps, not architectural gaps, but they affect the system's reliability.

The frontend's zero-build approach (single HTML file) is architecturally elegant. It means the web UI is a static artifact that can be served by any HTTP server — Node.js, nginx, Apache, or even a file:// URL. There's no build output to manage, no source maps to maintain, no asset hashing to configure.

The test infrastructure (vitest) is well-integrated. The test command runs synchronously, tests import directly from src/, and no pre-compilation is needed. This fast feedback loop encourages frequent testing.

For future CI/CD, the architecture should support: (1) GitHub Actions for automated testing on push/PR, (2) automated npm publishing on release tags, (3) Docker image building for container deployment, (4) automated security scanning (npm audit, Snyk).
variants.practitioner:
The build process is minimal and fast: npm run build runs tsc (compiles src/ to dist/), npm test runs vitest run (executes all tests), and npm publish runs the prepublishOnly hook (build + test) before publishing to npm. The entire build completes in 2-5 seconds on a modern machine.

For development, the workflow is: (1) Edit files in src/, (2) run 'npm test' to verify changes (vitest handles TypeScript directly), (3) run 'npm run build' only before publishing, (4) test the CLI: 'node dist/cli/index.js --help'.

The test suite has 112+ tests across tests/unit/. Run the full suite with npx vitest run, or run a specific test file with npx vitest run tests/unit/phase3.test.ts.

For CI/CD setup, create .github/workflows/test.yml with a matrix strategy testing Node.js 18, 20, and 22 on ubuntu-latest. Steps: checkout, setup-node, npm ci, npm test, npm run build.

Package distribution files (package.json files field): dist/ (compiled JavaScript) and prompt-framework/ (framework JSON files). These are included in the npm package; everything else is excluded.

The dist/ output preserves the src/ directory structure. Import paths in the compiled JS use .js extensions matching the TypeScript source imports. The CLI entry point is dist/cli/index.js, referenced in the package.json bin field as the 'space' command.
variants.strategist:
The simple build approach is strategically appropriate for SPACE's current stage. A solo-developer project doesn't need GitOps, automated staging environments, or complex deployment pipelines. The manual build-and-publish process is fast (2-5 seconds) and has a proven safety net (prepublishOnly hook). Adding CI/CD infrastructure at this stage would create overhead without proportional value.

However, the absence of CI/CD creates a scalability bottleneck. As the project grows (more contributors, more features, more tests), the manual build process will become a bottleneck. The Docker image option is strategically valuable for two use cases: (1) CI/CD environments where developers want to run SPACE in a pipeline, and (2) cloud development environments (Codespaces, Gitpod) where SPACE needs to run alongside other tools.
